summary.content: The authors express gratitude to Todd Coleman for discussions and acknowledge support from the Beckman Fellowship. They consider a scenario where the set of compressed observations is a singleton, leading to the definition of an $n$-tuple $W^n$ and a function $J = e_n(X^n,Y^n)$. Through a series of inequalities based on information-theoretic principles, they derive that the expected loss $\E L(\wh{f}_n,P)$ is bounded below by the divergence $D_{Y|X}(R,P)$ as $n$ approaches infinity. This indicates that the information-theoretic lower bound is less stringent than the bound derived from the expected loss, establishing a relationship between the two in the context of rate-constrained learning.

paper.title:
Sensor Networks with Random Links: Topology Design for Distributed
  Consensus
paper.author: Soummya Kar, Jos\'e M.~F.~Moura$^*

sections.content: We consider the design of the optimal topology, i.e., the communication configuration of a sensor network that maximizes the convergence rate of average consensus. Average consensus is a distributed algorithm that has been considered by Tsitsiklis in his PhD thesis, , see also~, found application recently in several areas, and is the subject of active research, e.g,,. This topology design for sensor networks has not received much attention in the literature. References~ and~ consider restrict it to classes of random graphs, in particular, small-world topologies. The more general question of designing the topology that maximizes the convergence rate, under a constraint on the number of network links, was considered in our previous work, , where we reduced to average consensus the problem of distributed inference in sensor networks; see also~. Realistic networks operate under stress: inparaenum[(1)] - noise and errors cause links to fail at random times; - communication among sensors entails a cost; and - scarcity of resources constrain sensors and networks operation. inparaenum We model such a non-deterministic network topology as a random field. Specifically, we assume the following: inparaenum[1)] - at each iteration of the consensus algorithm, a network link is active with some probability, referred to as link formation or utilization probability; - network links have different link formation probabilities; - links fail or are alive independently of each other; and - the link formation probabilities remain constant across iterations. inparaenum Designing the network topology corresponds then to inparaenum[(1)] - fixing the probability, or fraction of time, each link is used, - knowing that communication among sensors may be cheap (e.g., sensors are geographically close), or expensive, and - recognizing that there is an overall budget constraint taxing the communication in the network. inparaenum The paper extends our preliminary convergence results, , on networks with random links. The recent paper~ adopts a similar model and analyzes convergence properties using ergodicity of stochastic matrices. Consensus with a randomized network also relates to gossip algorithms, , where only a single pair of randomly selected sensors is allowed to communicate at each iteration, and the communication exchanged by the nodes is averaged. In our randomized consensus, we use multiple randomly selected links at each iteration and, in contradistinction with~, we design the optimal topology, i.e., the optimal weight (not simple average) and the optimal probabilities of edge utilization, recognizing that communication entails costs, and that there is a communication cost constraint. Other recent work on evolving topologies includes~ that considers continuous time consensus in networks with switching topologies and communication delays, and~ that studies distributed consensus when the network is a complete graph with identical link failure probabilities on all links. - Assuming the random link failure model discussed above, - We then show that higher - We outline the paper. Section~ summarizes spectral graph theory concepts like the graph Laplacian~$L$ and the graph algebraic connectivity $\lambda_2(L)$. The Section formulates the problem of distributed average consensus with random link failures. Sections~ and derive necessary and sufficient conditions for convergence of the mean state, mss convergence, and a.s.~convergence in terms of the average $\mbox{E}\left\{\lambda_2\left(L\right)\right\}$ and in terms of $\lambda_{2}\left(\overline{L}\right)$, where $\overline{L}=\mbox{E}\left(L\right)$. Section~ presents bounds on the mss convergence rate. Section~ addresses the topology design for random networks with communication cost constraints. We formulate a first version of the problem, the randomized distributed consensus with a communication cost constraint (RCCC), and then an alternate version, which we show is a convex constrained optimization problem, to which we apply semidefinite programming~(SDP) techniques. Section~ studies the performance of the topologies found by solving numerically the SDP optimization. We show that these designs can improve significantly the convergence rate, for example, by a factor of~$3$, when compared to geometric networks (networks where sensors communicate with every other sensor within a fixed radius) and that they can achieve practically the (asymptotic) performance of a nonrandom network at a fraction, e.g., 50~ paper. - fixed topology; - random topology; - random with communication costs topology.

summary.content: The paper addresses the design of optimal topologies for sensor networks to enhance the convergence rate of average consensus, a distributed algorithm previously explored by Tsitsiklis. It highlights the lack of attention given to topology design in the literature, particularly in the context of random graphs and small-world topologies. The authors model the network as a random field, incorporating factors such as varying link formation probabilities and independent link failures. They propose a framework for optimizing the network topology under communication cost constraints, utilizing semidefinite programming techniques, and demonstrate that their designs can significantly improve convergence rates compared to traditional geometric networks. The paper outlines the necessary conditions for convergence and presents bounds on the convergence rate, emphasizing the practical implications of their findings.

Subsection~ presents two network models: inparaenum[Model 1)] - Nonrandom topology in paragraph~; and - Random topology in paragraph~.inparaenum \ Subsection~ considers distributed average consensus with nonrandom topologies in Paragraph~ and random topologies in Paragraph~. We assume synchronous communication throughout. Nonrandom and Random Topologies In a nonrandom topology, the communication channels stay available whenever the sensors need to communicate. This model is described in paragraph~, where we recall basic concepts from graph theory. In many sensor network applications, it makes sense to consider that links among sensors may fail or become alive at random times. This models, for example, applications when the network uses an ARQ protocol and no acknowledgement packet is received within the protocol time window, in which case the transmitted packet is assumed to be dropped or lost. This is also the case, when the transmission is detected in error. The random topology introduced in paragraph~ models these networks. Nonrandom topology The nonrandom topology is defined by an undirected graph $G=(V,\mathcal{E})$, where $V$ is the set of vertices that model the sensors and $\mathcal{E}$ is the set of edges that model the communication channels. We refer to~$G$ as the supergraph, $\mathcal{E}$ as the superset of edges, and edges in $\mathcal{E}$ as realizable edges or links. This terminology becomes better motivated when we consider the random topology in Subsection~. The cardinalities of the sets $|V|=N$ and $|\mathcal{E}|=M$ give the number of network sensors and the number of channels or links, respectively. For the complete graph $G=(V,\mathcal{M})$, $\mathcal{M}$ is the set of all possible $N(N-1)/2$ edges. In practice, we are interested in sparse graphs, i.e., $M\ll N(N-1)/2$. We label a node or vertex by an integer $n$, where $n\in \{1,...,N\}$. Sensors~$n$ and~$l$ communicate if there is an edge $(n,l)\in\mathcal{E}$. Since the graph is undirected, if~$n$ communicates with~$l$, then~$l$ communicates with~$n$. The graph is called simple if it is devoid of loops (self-edges) and multiple edges. It is connected if every vertex can be reached from any other vertex, which in network terms may require a routing protocol. The number $d_n$ of edges connected to vertex~$n$ is called the degree of the vertex. A graph is regular if every vertex has the same degree~$d$. Unless otherwise stated, we consider only simple, connected graphs. Associated with the graph~$G$ is its $N	imes N$ adjacency matrix~$\mathcal{A}$  egin{equation} \label{A_def} \mathcal{A}_{nl} = \left\{  egin{array}{ll}  1 & \mbox{if $(n,l) \in \mathcal{E}$} \  0 & \mbox{otherwise}  \end{array}  ight. \end{equation} The neighborhood structure of the graph is defined by  egin{equation} \label{neighborhood}  orall 1\leq n\leq N:\:\:\Omega _{n} = \left\{l\in V:~(n,l)\in \mathcal{E}ight\} \end{equation} The degree of node~$n$ is also the cardinality of its neighborhood set  egin{equation} \label{deg_def}  orall 1\leq n\leq N:\:\:\mbox{d}_{n}=|\Omega _{n}| \end{equation} Let $\mathcal{D} = \mbox{diag}(\mbox{d}_{1},...,\mbox{d}_{N})$ be the degree matrix. The graph Laplacian matrix~$\mathcal{L}$ is defined as  egin{equation} \label{L_def} \mathcal{L} = \mathcal{D}-\mathcal{A} \end{equation} The Laplacian~$\mathcal{L}$ is a symmetric positive-semidefinite matrix; hence, all its eigenvalues are non-negative. We order the Laplacian eigenvalues as  egin{equation} \label{lambdamathcalL} 0=\lambda_{1}(\mathcal{L})\leq\lambda_{2}(\mathcal{L})\leq \cdots\leq\lambda_{N}(\mathcal{L}) \end{equation} The multiplicity of the zero eigenvalue of the Laplacian is equal to the number of connected components of the graph. Thus, for a connected graph, $\lambda_{2}(\mathcal{L})>0$. In the literature, $\lambda_{2}(\mathcal{L})$ is referred to as the algebraic connectivity (or Fiedler value) of the network (see~.) The normalized eigenvector $\mathbf{u}_1(\mathcal{L})$ corresponding to the zero eigenvalue is the normalized vector of ones  egin{equation} \label{eq:vector1} \mathbf{u}_1\left(\mathcal{L}ight)= rac{1}{\sqrt{N}}\mathbf{1}=\left[ rac{1}{\sqrt{N}}\cdots rac{1}{\sqrt{N}}ight]^T \end{equation} For additional concepts from graph theory see~~. Random Topology We consider sensor networks where failures may occur at random due to noise as when packets are dropped. If a link fails at time~$i$, it can come back online at a later time (a failed transmission may be succeeded by a successful one.) We describe a graph model for this random topology. We start with the model in paragraph~ of a simple, connected supergraph $G=\left(V,\mathcal{E}ight)$ with $|V|=N$ and $|\mathcal{E}|=M$. The superset of edges $\mathcal{E}$ collects the realizable edges, i.e., the channels that are established directly among sensors in the network when all realizable links are online. These channels may fail at random times, but if $(n,l)
otin\mathcal{E}$ then sensors~$n$ and~$l$ do not communicate directly---of course, they still communicate by rerouting their messages through one of the paths connecting them in~$G$, since~$G$ is connected. We now construct the model for the random topology problem, see also. To model this network with random link failures, we assume that the state, failed or online, of each link $(n,l)\in\mathcal{E}$ over time $i=1,\cdots$ is a Bernoulli process with probability of formation $P_{nl}$, i.e., the probability of failure at time~$i$ is $1-P_{nl}$. We assume that for any realizable edges $(n,l)
eq(m,k)$ the corresponding Bernoulli processes are statistically independent. Under this model, at each time~$i$, the the resulting topology is described by a graph $G(i)=\left(V,E(i)ight)$. The edge set $E(i)$ and the adjacency matrix~$A(i)$ are random, with $E(i)$ and $E(j)$, as well as $A(i)$ and $A(j)$, statistically independent, identically distributed (iid) for $i
eq j$. Note that $E(i)\subset\mathcal{E}$ and $0 A(i)$, where $0$ is the $N N$ zero matrix and $C\preceq D$ stands for $ 1 i,j N: C_i,j D_i,j$. We can think of the set $E(i)$ as an instantiation of a random binary valued $M$-tuple. The probability of a particular instantiation $E(i)$ is $\Pi_{(n,l)\in\mathcal{E}}P_{nl}$. We collect the edge formation probabilities in the edge formation probability matrix \[ P=P^T=[P_nl], P_n,n=0 \] The diagonal elements are zero because the graph is simple (no loops). The structure of~$P$ reflects the structure of the adjacency matrix~$\mathcal{A}$ of the superset~$\mathcal{E}$, i.e., $P_{nl}
eq0$ if and only if $\mathcal{A}_{nl}=1$. The matrix~$P$ is not stochastic; its elements are $0\leq P_{nl}\leq 1$ but their row or column sums are not normalized to~$1$. Abusing notation, we will refer to~$P$ as the probability distribution of the~$E(i)$ and~$A(i)$. We now consider the average consensus algorithm for both nonrandom and random topologies. Average Consensus We overview average consensus, see and also for recent work. It computes by a distributed algorithm the average of $x_n(0)$, $n=1,\cdots,N$ where $x_n(0)$ is available at sensor~$n$. At time~$i$, each node exchanges its state $x_n(i)$, $i=0,1,\cdots$ synchronously with its neighbors specified by the graph edge neighborhood set, see eqn.~(). In vector form, the $N$ states $x_n(i)$ are collected in the state vector $\mathbf{x}(i)\in\mathbb{R}^{N	imes 1}$. Define the average $\overline{r}$ and the vector of averages $\mathbf{x}_{\mbox{\scriptsize avg}}$  egin{eqnarray} \label{eqn:averager} \overline{r}&=& rac{1}{N}\mathbf{1}^{T}\mathbf{x}(0)\ \label{def_xavg} \mathbf{x}_{\mbox{\scriptsize avg}} &=&\overline{r}\mathbf{1}\ \label{def_xavg-b} &=& rac{1}{N}\mathbf{1}\mathbf{1}^{T}\mathbf{x}(0)\ \label{def_xavg-c} &=& rac{1}{N}J\mathbf{x}(0) \end{eqnarray} and where~$\mathbf{1}$ is the vector of ones, see~(), and $J=\mathbf{1}\mathbf{1}^{T}$. We next consider the iterative average consensus algorithm for both nonrandom and random topologies. Average consensus: Nonrandom topology With the nonrandom topology defined by the supergraph $G=(V, E)$, the state update by the average consensus proceeds according to the iterative algorithm  egin{eqnarray} \label{lin_up_sens}  orall i\geq0:\:\:\:x_{n}(i+1)&=&\mathcal{W}_{nn}x_{n}(i)+\sum_{l\in\Omega_{n}}\mathcal{W}_{nl}x_{l}(i)\ \label{lin_up_mat} \mathbf{x}(i+1)&=&\mathcal{W}\mathbf{x}(i)\end{eqnarray} where: $\Omega_{n}$ is the neighborhood of sensor~$n$; $\mathbf{x}(i)$ is the state vector collecting all states $x_n(i)$, $1\leq n\leq N$; $\mathcal{W}_{nl}$ is the weight of edge $(n,l)$; and the matrix of weights is $\mathcal{W}=\left[\mathcal{W}_{nl}ight]$. The sparsity of~$W$ is determined by the underlying network connectivity, i.e., for $n
eq l$, the weight $\mathcal{W}_{nl}=0$ if $(n,l) E$. Iterating~(),  egin{eqnarray} \label{prod_x-a} \mathbf{x}(i) &=&\left(\prod_{j=0}^{i-1}\mathcal{W}ight)\mathbf{x}(0)\ \label{prod_x-b} &=&\mathcal{W}^i \mathbf{x}(0) \end{eqnarray} A common choice for the weight matrix~$\mathcal{W}$ is the equal weights matrix, ,  egin{equation} \label{cons_W-a}  \mathcal{W}=I-\alpha\mathcal{L} \end{equation} where $\mathcal{L}$ is the Laplacian associated with~$\mathcal{E}$, and $\alpha\geq 0$ is a constant independent of time $i$. For the equal weights matrix and a connected network, given the ordering~() of the eigenvalues of~$\mathcal{L}$, and that~$\alpha$ is nonnegative, the eigenvalues of~$\mathcal{W}$ can be reordered as  egin{equation}\label{Eq:lambdaW}  1=\lambda_1\left(\mathcal{W}ight)\geq\lambda_2\left(\mathcal{W}ight)\geq\cdots\geq\lambda_N\left(\mathcal{W}ight) \end{equation} The eigenvector corresponding to $\lambda_1\left(\mathcal{W}ight)$ is still the vector $\mathbf{u}_1\left(\mathcal{W}ight)= rac{1}{\sqrt{N}}\mathbf{1}$. Reference~ studies the problem of optimizing the nonzero weights~$\mathcal{W}_{nl}$ for maximizing convergence rate when the adjacency matrix~$\mathcal{A}$ is known. In particular, this reference shows that, for the equal weights case, fastest convergence is obtained with  egin{equation}\label{eq:equaloptimalweight}  \alpha^{*}= rac{2}{\lambda_2\left(\mathcal{L}ight)+\lambda_N\left(\mathcal{L}ight)} \end{equation} In~, we consider this equal weight~$\mathcal{W}$ and show that the class of non-bipartite Ramanujan graphs provides the optimal (nonrandom) topology under a constraint on the number of network links $M$, see also~. This optimality is in the asymptotic limit of large~$N$, see the references for details. Average consensus: Random topology At each time~$i$, the graph $G(i)=\left(V,E(i)ight)$ is random. The distributed average consensus algorithm still follows a vector iterative equation like~(), except now the weight matrices $W(i)$ are time dependent and random. We focus on the equal weights problem,  egin{equation} \label{cons_W} W(i) = I-\alpha L(i) \end{equation} where $L(i)$ is the Laplacian of the random network at time~$i$. The $L(i)$ are random iid matrices whose probability distribution is determined by the edge formation probability matrix~$P$. Likewise, the weight matrices $W(i)$, $i=0,1,...$ are also iid random matrices. We often drop the time index~$i$ in the random matrices~$L(i)$ and~$W(i)$ or their statistics. Iterating~() with this time dependent weight matrix leads to  egin{equation} \label{prod_x} \mathbf{x}(i) = \left(\prod_{j=0}^{i-1}W(j)ight)\mathbf{x}(0) \end{equation} Since the weights $W_{nl}$ are random, the state $\mathbf{x}(i)$ is also a random vector. Section~ analyzes the influence of the topology on the convergence properties as we iterate~().

summary.content: The section discusses distributed average consensus in sensor networks with both nonrandom and random topologies, assuming synchronous communication. In nonrandom topologies, communication channels are consistently available, modeled by an undirected graph where vertices represent sensors and edges represent communication links. The average consensus algorithm updates the state of each sensor based on its neighbors, using a weight matrix derived from the graph's Laplacian. In contrast, random topologies account for link failures modeled as Bernoulli processes, leading to time-dependent and random weight matrices. The iterative consensus process remains similar, but the resulting state vector becomes random due to the variability in the network topology over time.

sections.content:
Subsection~ describes the random topology model. The supergraph $G=\left(V,\mathcal{E}ight)$ is connected and~$P$ is the matrix of edge formation probabilities. Since the $A(i)$, $L(i)$, and $W(i)$ are iid  egin{eqnarray} % 
onumber to remove numbering (before each equation)  \overline{A} &=& E\left[A(i)ight] \  \overline{L} &=& E\left[L(i)ight] \  \overline{W} &=& E\left[W(i)ight]\  &=&I-\alpha \overline{L} \end{eqnarray} i.e., their means are time independent. We establish properties of the Laplacian, Subsection~, and weight matrices, Subsection~, needed when studying the random topology and random topology with communication cost constraint problems in sections~ through~. Laplacian We list some properties of the mean Laplacian and bound the expected value of the algebraic connectivity of the random Laplacians by the algebraic connectivity of the mean Laplacian. lemma The mean adjacency matrix~$\overline{A}$ and mean Laplacian are given by  egin{eqnarray}\label{A_bar} \overline{A}&=&P\ \label{L_bar} \overline{L}_{nl}&=&\left\{ egin{array}{ll}  \sum_{m=1}^{N}P_{nm} & \mbox{if $n=l$} \  -P_{nl} & \mbox{otherwise}  \end{array}  ight. \end{eqnarray} lemma This Lemma is straightforward to prove. From the Lemma, it follows that the mean adjacency matrix~$\overline{A}$ is not a $(0,1)$ matrix. Similarly. from the structure of the matrix $\overline{L}$, see eqn.~(), it follows that $\overline{L}$ can be interpreted as the weighted Laplacian of a graph $\overline{G}$ with non-negative link weights. In particular, the weight of the link $(n,l)$ of $\overline{G}$ is $P_{nl}$. The properties of the mean Laplacian are similar to the properties of the Laplacian. We state them in the following two Lemmas. lemma The mean Laplacian matrix $\overline{L}=\mbox{E}\left[L(j)ight],~j=0,1,...$ is positive semidefinite. Its eigenvalues can be arranged as  egin{equation} \label{eig_L_bar} 0=\lambda_{1}\left(\overline{L}ight)\leq\lambda_{2}\left(\overline{L}ight)\leq\cdots\leq\lambda_{N}\left(\overline{L}ight) \end{equation} where the normalized eigenvector associated with the zero eigenvalue $\lambda_{1}\left(\overline{L}ight)$ is  egin{equation} \label{eq:u1Lbar} \mathbf{u}_1\left(\overline{L}ight)= rac{1}{\sqrt{N}}\mathbf{1} \end{equation} lemma proof Let $\mathbf{z}\in\mathbb{R}^{N	imes 1}$ be a non-zero vector. Then, from eqn.~(), we have  egin{equation} \label{lemma-.1_1} \mathbf{z}^{T}\overline{L}\mathbf{z}=\sum_{n,l}\overline{L}_{nl}z_{n}z_{l}= rac{1}{2}\sum_{n
eq l}P_{nl}(z_{n}-z_{l})^{2} \end{equation} Since the $P_{nl}$'s are non-negative, $\overline{L}$ is positive semidefinite. Eqn.() follows readily from eqn.(). proof Interpreting $\overline{L}$ as the weighted Laplacian of the graph $\overline{G}$, we note that $\lambda_{2}\left(\overline{L}ight)=0$ implies that $\overline{G}$ is not connected (see~.) In other words, if $\lambda_{2}\left(\overline{L}ight)=0$, then $\overline{G}$ has at least two disconnected components; hence, $\overline{L}$ takes the form of a block diagonal matrix (after permuting the rows and columns). Such matrices are called reducible matrices. Also, it immediately follows (see~) that, if $\overline{L}$ is irreducible, then $\lambda_{2}\left(\overline{L}ight)
eq0$. Thus, we get the following Lemma. lemma Let the mean Laplacian be the weighted Laplacian for a graph~$\overline{G}$.  egin{equation} \label{th3.2} \lambda_{2}\left(\overline{L}ight)>0\Longleftrightarrow \mbox{$\overline{L}$ is irreducible}\Longleftrightarrow \overline{G}\:\mbox{is connected} \end{equation}lemma The convergence results in Section~ on the average consensus involve the mean $\mbox{E}\left[\lambda_{2}(L)ight]$, which is manifestly difficult to compute. A much easier quantity to compute is $\lambda_{2}\left(\overline{L}ight)$. We relate here the two. First, we show that $\lambda_{2}(L)$ is a concave function of $L$. lemma $\lambda_{2}(L)$ is a concave function of $L$. lemma proof From the Courant-Fisher Theorem (see~)  egin{equation} \label{l6.1} \lambda_{2}(L)=\min_{\mathbf{z} ot\mathbf{1}} rac{\mathbf{z}^{T}L\mathbf{z}}{\mathbf{z}^{T}\mathbf{z}} \end{equation} Then for any two Laplacians $L_{1}$ and $L_{2}$ and $0 t 1$ we have  egin{eqnarray} \label{l6.2} \lambda_{2}(tL_{1}+(1-t)L_{2}) & = & \min_{\mathbf{z} ot\mathbf{1}} rac{\mathbf{z}^{T}(tL_{1}+(1-t)L_{2})\mathbf{z}}{\mathbf{z}^{T}\mathbf{z}} \ 
onumber & \geq & t\min_{\mathbf{z} ot\mathbf{1}} rac{\mathbf{z}^{T}L_{1}\mathbf{z}}{\mathbf{z}^{T}\mathbf{z}} + (1-t)\min_{\mathbf{z} ot\mathbf{1}} rac{\mathbf{z}^{T}L_{2}\mathbf{z}}{\mathbf{z}^{T}\mathbf{z}} \ 
onumber & = & t\lambda_{2}(L_{1})+(1-t)\lambda_{2}(L_{2}) \end{eqnarray} Thus $\lambda_{2}(L)$ is a concave function of $L$. proof lemma  egin{equation} \label{rel_mom} \mbox{E}\left[\lambda_{2}(L)ight]\leq\lambda_{2}\left(\overline{L}ight) \end{equation} lemma proof Follows from Lemma~ and Jensen's inequality. proof Weight matrices We consider properties of the (random and mean) weight matrices. lemma The eigenvalues of $\overline{W}$ are  egin{eqnarray} \label{eig_W_bar} 1\leq j\leq N:&&\lambda_{j}\left(\overline{W}ight)=1-\alpha\lambda_{j}\left(\overline{L}ight)\ \label{eig_W_bar_1} 1&=&\lambda_{1}\left(\overline{W}ight)\geq \lambda_{2}\left(\overline{W}ight)\cdots\geq\lambda_{N}\left(\overline{W}ight) \end{eqnarray} The eigenvector corresponding to the eigenvalue $\lambda_{1}\left(\overline{W}ight)$ is  egin{equation} \label{eq:u1overlineW} \mathbf{u}_1\left(\overline{W}ight)= rac{1}{\sqrt{N}}\mathbf{1} \end{equation} Similar results hold for~$W(i)$. lemma This Lemma follows immediately from the corresponding results on the mean Laplacian and the~$L(i)$. We now consider results on the spectral norm and its expected value for the random matrices $W(i)$ and their mean~$\overline{W}$. These results are used when studying convergence of the average consensus in Section~. lemma Let $\mathbf{z}\in\mathbb{R}^{N	imes 1}$ and $ ()$ be the spectral radius. Then  egin{equation} \label{lemma-.4_1}  orall \:W(j):\:\: \left\|W(j)\mathbf{z}- rac{1}{N}J\mathbf{z}ight\|\leqho\left (W(j)- rac{1}{N}Jight)\left\|\mathbf{z}- rac{1}{N}J\mathbf{z}ight\| \end{equation} lemma proof Decompose $W(j)$ through orthonormal eigenvectors as $W(j)=U(j)\Lambda(j) U(j)^{T}$. From eqn.~(), $\lambda_{1}(W(j))=1$ with normalized eigenvector $\mathbf{u}_{1}(j)= rac{1}{\sqrt{N}}\mathbf{1}$. Hence,  egin{equation} \label{l2.2} \mathbf{z}= rac{1}{N}J\mathbf{z}+\sum_{k=2}^{N}c_{k}(j)\mathbf{u}_{k}(j) \end{equation} where $c_{k}(j)=\mathbf{u}_{k}(j)^{T}\mathbf{z},~k=2,...,N$. Then  egin{equation} \label{l2.3} W(j)\mathbf{z} = rac{1}{N}J\mathbf{z}+\sum_{k=2}^{N}c_{k}(j)\lambda_{k}(W(j))\mathbf{u}_{k}(j) \end{equation} It follows that  egin{eqnarray} \label{l2.4} \left\| W(j)\mathbf{z}- rac{1}{N}J\mathbf{z}ight\| & = & \left\| \sum_{k=2}^{N}c_{k}(j)\lambda_{k}(W(j))\mathbf{u}_{k}(j)ight\|\ 
onumber & \leq & ho \left(W(j)- rac{1}{N}Jight) \left\| \sum_{k=2}^{N}c_{k}(j)\mathbf{u}_{k}(j)ight\|\ 
onumber & = & ho \left(W(j)- rac{1}{N}Jight)\left\| \mathbf{z}- rac{1}{N}J\mathbf{z}ight\| \end{eqnarray} This proves the Lemma. proof lemma We have  egin{eqnarray} \label{def_rho} ho\left(\overline{W}- rac{1}{N}Jight)&=&\max \left(|\lambda_{2}\left(\overline{W}ight)|,|\lambda_{N}\left(\overline{W}ight)|ight) = \max\left(\lambda_{2}\left(\overline{W}ight),-\lambda_{N}\left(\overline{W}ight)ight)\ \label{def_rho-wi} ho\left(W(i)- rac{1}{N}Jight)&=&\max \left(|\lambda_{2}\left(W(i)ight)|,|\lambda_{N}\left(W(i)ight)|ight) = \max\left(\lambda_{2}\left(W(i)ight),-\lambda_{N}\left(W(i)ight)ight) \end{eqnarray} lemma proof We prove only the Lemma for~$\overline{W}$. Matrix $ rac{1}{N}J$ is rank one, and the its non-zero eigenvalue is~$1$ with normalized eigenvector $ rac{1}{\sqrt{N}}\mathbf{1}$. Hence, from eqn.~(), the eigenvalues of $\left(\overline{W}- rac{1}{N}Jight)$ are~$0$ and $\lambda_{2}\left(\overline{W}ight),...,\lambda_{N}\left(\overline{W}ight)$. By the definition of spectral radius and eqn.~(),  egin{equation} \label{lemma-.2_1} ho \left(\overline{W}- rac{1}{N}Jight)=\max \left(0,|\lambda_{2}\left(\overline{W}ight)|,...,|\lambda_{N}\left(\overline{W}ight)|ight)=\max \left(|\lambda_{2}\left(\overline{W}ight)|,|\lambda_{N}\left(\overline{W}ight)|ight) \end{equation} Also, noting that $\lambda_{2}\left(\overline{W}ight)\geq\lambda_{N}\left(\overline{W}ight)$, it follows from eqn.~() that  egin{equation} \label{def_rho-b} ho \left(\overline{W}- rac{1}{N}Jight)=\max\left(\lambda_{2}\left(\overline{W}ight),-\lambda_{N}\left(\overline{W}ight)ight) \end{equation} proof We now consider the convexity of the spectral norm as a function of~$\alpha$ and~$L$. lemma For a given $L$, $ (W-1NJ)$ is a convex function of~$$. For a given $\alpha$, $ho \left(W- rac{1}{N}Jight)$ is a convex function of~$L$. lemma proof We prove the convexity with respect to~$\alpha$ only. Let $\alpha_{1},\alpha_{2}\in\mathbb{R}$ and $0\leq t\leq 1$. For symmetric matrices the spectral radius is equal to the matrix 2-norm. We get  egin{eqnarray} 
onumber ho \left(I-\left(t\alpha_{1}+(1-t)\alpha_{2}ight)L- rac{1}{N}Jight) & = & \left\| I - t\alpha_{1}L-(1-t)\alpha_{2}L - rac{1}{N}Jight\|_{2} \ 
onumber & = & \left\|t\left(I-\alpha_{1}L- rac{1}{N}Jight)+(1-t)\left(I-\alpha_{2}L- rac{1}{N}Jight)ight\|_{2}\ 
onumber & \leq & \left\|t\left(I-\alpha_{1}L- rac{1}{N}Jight)ight\|_{2}+ \left\|(1-t)\left(I-\alpha_{2}L- rac{1}{N}Jight)ight\|_{2}\ \label{l4.1} & = & tho \left(I-\alpha_{1}L- rac{1}{N}Jight) + (1-t)ho \left(I-\alpha_{2}L- rac{1}{N}Jight) \end{eqnarray} that proves the Lemma. proof The next Lemma considers the convexity of the expected value of the spectral norm, taken over the probability distribution of the Laplacian. The following Lemma bounds $E[ (W-1NJ)]$. lemma For a given probability distribution (and hence $P$) of $L$, $\mbox{E}\left[ho\left(W- rac{1}{N}Jight)ight]$ is convex on~$\alpha$. lemma proof The convexity of $\mbox{E}\left[ho\left(W- rac{1}{N}Jight)ight]$ follows from Lemma~, eqn.~(), and the properties of Lebesgue integration. proof lemma For a given choice of $\alpha$,  egin{equation} \label{l3.1} \mbox{E}\left[ho \left(W- rac{1}{N}Jight)ight]\geq ho \left(\overline{W}- rac{1}{N}Jight) \end{equation} lemma proof The Lemma follows from Lemma~ and Jensen's inequality. proof

summary.content: The section discusses the random topology model for sensor networks, focusing on the properties of the mean adjacency matrix $\overline{A}$ and mean Laplacian $\overline{L}$. It establishes that $\overline{L}$ is positive semidefinite, with eigenvalues arranged such that $\lambda_{1}(\overline{L}) = 0$ indicates a disconnected graph. The relationship between the algebraic connectivity of the random Laplacians and the mean Laplacian is explored, showing that $\lambda_{2}(L)$ is a concave function of $L$. Additionally, it examines the spectral properties of the weight matrices, concluding that the expected spectral norm is convex with respect to the probability distribution of the Laplacian.

sections.section_title: Convergence of Average Consensus: Random Topology
sections.content:
For average consensus in random topologies, we start by considering the convergence of the state  egin{equation} \label{conv_x}  orall\mathbf{x}(0)\in\mathbb{R}^{N	imes 1}:\:\:\lim_{iightarrow\infty}\mathbf{x}(i)=\mathbf{x}_{\mbox{\scriptsize{avg}}} \end{equation} in some appropriate probabilistic sense. Subsection~ studies convergence of the mean vector, $\mbox{E}\left[\mathbf{x}(i)ight]$, Subsection~ considers convergence in the mean-square-sense~(mss), and almost sure convergence (convergence with probability 1) is treated in Subsection~. Mean state convergence The sequence of expected state vectors converges if  egin{equation} \label{convcond_Ex} \lim_{iightarrow\infty}\left\| \mbox{E}\mathbf{x}(i)-\mathbf{x}_{\mbox{\scriptsize{avg}}}ight\| = 0 \end{equation} For simplicity, we assume $\|\cdot\|$ to be the $\mathcal{L}_{2}$-norm. We analyze the convergence of the mean state vector in ~ and then study the topology that optimizes its convergence rate in~. Mean state convergence The mean state evolution is given in the following Lemma. lemma Recall $\mathbf{x}_{\mbox{\scriptsize{avg}}}$ given in~(). Then  egin{equation} \label{Ex_avg} \mbox{E}\mathbf{x}(i)-\mathbf{x}_{\mbox{\scriptsize{avg}}}=\left(\overline{W}- rac{1}{N}Jight)^{i}(\mathbf{x}(0)-\mathbf{x}_{\mbox{\scriptsize{avg}}}) \end{equation} lemma proof Using eqn.~() and the fact that the matrices~$W(i)$ are iid  egin{equation} \label{Ex} \mbox{E}\left[\mathbf{x}(i)ight]=\overline{W}^{i}\mathbf{x}(0) \end{equation} The Lemma follows by recalling that $\mathbf{1}$ is an eigenvector of $\overline{W}$. proof Convergence of the mean is now straightforward. theorem A necessary and sufficient condition for the mean to converge is  egin{equation} \label{Ex_conv_cond} ho \left(\overline{W}- rac{1}{N}Jight)<1 \end{equation} theorem proof Lemma~ shows that the convergence of the mean is equivalent to deterministic distributed average consensus. The necessary and sufficient condition for convergence then follows from references~. proof Fastest mean convergence topology We introduce the definition of convergence factor. definition[Mean convergence factor] If $ho\left(\overline{W}- rac{1}{N}Jight)<1$, we call $ (W-1NJ)$ the mean convergence factor of the consensus algorithm. definition For fastest mean convergence, $ (W-1NJ)$ should be as small as possible. Hence, the optimal topology with respect to convergence of the mean state vector is the topology that minimizes this convergence factor. We address this problem in the following two Theorems. We note that $ho (\overline{W}- rac{1}{J}N)$ is a function of both $\alpha$ and $\overline{L}$. In the following Theorem, we state conditions on $\overline{L}$ that guarantee that we can choose an $\alpha$ for which there is convergence of the mean. theorem A necessary condition for the mean to converge is  egin{equation} \label{eq:necessarymean} \lambda_{2}\left(\overline{L}ight)>0 \end{equation} A sufficient condition is~() and  egin{equation} \label{Ex_alpha_bound}0<\alpha<2/\lambda_{N}\left(\overline{L}ight) \end{equation} theorem proof We first prove the necessary condition by contradiction. Let $\lambda_{2}\left(\overline{L}ight)=0$. From eqn.~(), it follows that $\lambda_{2}\left(\overline{W}ight)=1$. Then, from eqn.~(), we have $ (W-1NJ) 1$, for every choice of $\alpha$. Hence, from Lemma~, it follows that, if $\lambda_{2}\left(\overline{L}ight)=0$, the mean vector does not converge for any choice of $\alpha$. This proves the necessary condition. For sufficiency, we assume that $\lambda_{2}\left(\overline{L}ight)>0$. Then, generalizing the results in~ to non-binary $(0-1)$ matrices, it can be shown that \[ (W-1NJ)<1 iff 0<<2/\lambda_N(L) \] which then guarantees convergence of the mean state vector. proof If $\lambda_{2}\left(\overline{L}ight)>0$, Theorem~ and eqn.~() give the values of $\alpha$ that lead to the convergence of the mean vector in terms of $\lambda_{N}\left(\overline{L}ight)$, a quantity easily evaluated since $\overline{L}$ is given by eqn.~(). The following Theorem gives the choice of $\alpha$ leading to the fastest convergence of the mean. theorem Let $\lambda_{2}\left(\overline{L}ight)>0$. Then the choice of $\alpha$ that minimizes $ (W-1NJ)$ and hence maximizes the convergence rate of the mean state vector is  egin{equation} \label{eq:alphamax} \alpha^{\star} = rac{2}{\lambda_{2}\left(\overline{L}ight)+\lambda_{N}\left(\overline{L}ight)} \end{equation} The corresponding minimum $ho(\cdot)$ is  egin{equation} \label{eq:rhomin} ho_{\mbox{\scriptsize min}}\left(\overline{W}- rac{1}{N}Jight) =  rac{1-\lambda_{2}\left(\overline{L}ight)/\lambda_{N}\left(\overline{L}ight)}{1+ \lambda_{2}\left(\overline{L}ight)/\lambda_{N}\left(\overline{L}ight)} \end{equation} theorem proof It follows by generalizing the result in~ to non-binary matrices. proof This section derived necessary and sufficient conditions for the convergence of the mean in terms of $\lambda_{2}\left(\overline{L}ight)$. Also, it provided the values of $\alpha$ that guarantee convergence when $\lambda_{2}\left(\overline{L}ight)>0$. The next Subsection considers mss convergence of average consensus. Mean Square Convergence This Section studies mean-square convergence, which implies convergence of the mean, but not the reverse. We say that the algorithm converges in the mean-square sense~(mss) iff  egin{equation} \label{def_mss_conv}  orall\mathbf{x}(0)\in\mathbb{R}^{N	imes 1}:\:\:\lim_{iightarrow\infty} \mbox{E}\left\|\mathbf{x}(i)-\mathbf{x}_{\mbox{\scriptsize{avg}}}ight\| = 0 \end{equation} We need the following lemma first. lemma For any $\mathbf{x}(0)\in\mathbb{R}^{N	imes 1}$  egin{equation} \label{l2.1} \left\|\mathbf{x}(i+1)-\mathbf{x}_{\mbox{\scriptsize{avg}}}ight\|~\leq \left(\prod_{j=0}^{i}ho\left(W(j)- rac{1}{N}Jight)ight)\left\|\mathbf{x}(0)-\mathbf{x}_{\mbox{\scriptsize{avg}}}ight\| \end{equation} lemma proof We have  egin{eqnarray} \label{l2.5} \left\|\mathbf{x}(i+1)-\mathbf{x}_{\mbox{\scriptsize{avg}}}ight\| & = & \left\|\left(\prod_{j=0}^{i}W(j)ight)\mathbf{x}(0)- rac{1}{N}J\mathbf{x}(0)ight\| \ 
onumber & = & \left\| W(i)\left(\prod_{j=0}^{i-1}W(j)\mathbf{x}(0)ight)- rac{1}{N}J\left(\prod_{j=0}^{i-1}W(j)\mathbf{x}(0)ight)ight\| \end{eqnarray} where we have used the fact that \[ 1NJ(\prod_j=0^i-1W(j)x(0))=1NJx(0) \] From Lemma~, it then follows  egin{eqnarray} \label{l2.10} \left\|\mathbf{x}(i+1)-\mathbf{x}_{\mbox{\scriptsize{avg}}}ight\|  & \leq & ho\left(W(i)- rac{1}{N}Jight)\left\|\left(\prod_{j=0}^{i-1}W(j)\mathbf{x}(0)ight)-   rac{1}{N}J\left(\prod_{j=0}^{i-1}W(j)\mathbf{x}(0)ight)ight\|\ 
onumber & = & ho\left(W(i)- rac{1}{N}Jight)\left\|\mathbf{x}(i)-\mathbf{x}_{\mbox{\scriptsize{avg}}}ight\| \end{eqnarray} Repeating the same argument for $j=0 \:\mbox{to}\: i$ we finally get  egin{equation} \label{l2.6} \left\|\mathbf{x}(i+1)-\mathbf{x}_{\mbox{\scriptsize{avg}}}ight\|~\leq \left(\prod_{j=0}^{i}ho\left(W(j)- rac{1}{N}Jight)ight)\left\|\mathbf{x}(0)-\mathbf{x}_{\mbox{\scriptsize{avg}}}ight\| \end{equation} This proves the Lemma. proof The following Theorem gives a sufficient condition for mss convergence. theorem If $\mbox{E}\left[ho\left(W- rac{1}{N}Jight)ight]<1$, the state vector sequence $\{\mathbf{x}(i)\}_{i=0}^{\infty}$ converges in the mss  egin{equation} \label{th2.1} \lim_{iightarrow\infty}\mbox{E}\left\|\mathbf{x}(i)-\mathbf{x}_{\mbox{\scriptsize{avg}}}ight\| = 0,~ orall\mathbf{x}(0)\in\mathbb{R}^{N	imes 1} \end{equation} theorem proof Taking expectation on both sides of eqn.~() in Lemma~ and using the iid of the $W(j)$'s  egin{equation} \label{th2.2} \mbox{E}\left\| \mathbf{x}_{i}-\mathbf{x}_{\mbox{\scriptsize{avg}}}ight\|~\leq \left(\mbox{E}\left[ho \left(W- rac{1}{N}Jight)ight]ight)^{i-1}\left\|\mathbf{x}_{0}-\mathbf{x}_{\mbox{\scriptsize{avg}}}ight\| \end{equation} where we dropped the index~$i$ in~$W(i)$. The Theorem then follows. proof Like the Definition~ for mean convergence factor, we introduce the mss convergence factor. First, note that $E[ (W-1NJ)]$ is a function of the weight $\alpha$ and the probability of edge formation matrix $P$ (or $\overline{L}$ from~().) definition[mss convergence factor, mss convergence rate] If $E[ (W-1NJ)]<1$, call $C\left(\alpha,\overline{L}ight)$ and $S_{\mbox{\scriptsize{g}}}(\alpha,\overline{L})$ the mss convergence factor and the mss convergence gain per iteration (or the mss convergence rate), respectively, where  egin{eqnarray} \label{eq:mssconvergencefactor} C\left(\alpha,\overline{L}ight)&=&\mbox{E}\left[ho \left(W- rac{1}{N}Jight)ight]\ \label{def_Sg} S_{\mbox{\scriptsize{g}}}(\alpha,\overline{L}) &=&-\ln\,\, C\left(\alpha,\overline{L}ight)\ \label{def_Sg-b} &=& \ln\left( rac{1}{\mbox{E}\left[ho \left(W- rac{1}{N}Jight)ight]}ight) \end{eqnarray} definition corollary mss convergence cannot be faster than convergence of the mean vector. corollary The Corollary follows from the Theorem and Lemma~. Theorem~ shows that the smaller the mss~convergence factor $C(,L)=E[ (W-1NJ)]$ is, the faster the mss~convergence. The actual value of $C\left(\alpha,\overline{L}ight)$ depends both on the probability distribution of the Laplacian~$L$ and the constant weight~$\alpha$. However, the probability distribution of~$L$ must satisfy certain conditions to guarantee that there are values of~$\alpha$ that lead to mss convergence. Otherwise, no choice of~$\alpha$ will result in mss~convergence. The next Theorem considers this issue. Before stating the Theorem, let $d_{\mbox{\scriptsize{max}}}$ be the maximum degree of the graph with edge set $E=\mathcal{E}$ and define  egin{equation} \label{th3.6} \alpha_{\mbox{\scriptsize{mss}}} =  rac{1}{2d_{\mbox{\scriptsize{max}}}} \end{equation} theorem There is an $\alpha$ such that the consensus algorithm converges in mss iff $\lambda_{2}\left(\overline{L}ight)>0$. In other words, if $\lambda_{2}\left(\overline{L}ight)>0$, we can find an $\alpha$, in particular, $\alpha=\alpha_{\mbox{\scriptsize mss}}$ defined in~(), that leads to mss~convergence. If $\lambda_{2}\left(\overline{L}ight)=0$, no choice of $\alpha$ will result in mss~convergence. theorem proof We first prove the sufficiency part. The proof is constructive, and we show that, if $\lambda_{2}\left(\overline{L}ight)>0$, we can find an $\alpha$ for which \[ C(,L)=E[(W-JN)]<1 \] Convergence then follows from Theorem~. Let $\lambda_{2}\left(\overline{L}ight)>0$. By Lemma~, $\overline{L}$ is irreducible. From irreducibility of $\overline{L}$, with non-zero probability, we have graph realizations for which~$L$ is irreducible and so $\lambda_{2}(L)>0$. In particular, with non-zero probability, we can have a realization for which the edge set $E=\mathcal{E}$; by assumption, this network is irreducible and hence connected (because the corresponding Laplacian matrix has the same sparsity pattern of $\overline{L}$ with non-zero entries of $\overline{L}$ replaced by ones.) Hence, with non-zero probability, $\lambda_{2}(L)>0$, which makes $\mbox{E}\left[\lambda_{2}(L)ight]>0$. Thus we have  egin{equation} \label{th3.3} \lambda_{2}\left(\overline{L}ight)>0\Longrightarrow \mbox{E}\left[\lambda_{2}(L)ight]>0 \end{equation} Let $d_{\mbox{\scriptsize{max}}}(G)$ be the maximum vertex degree of graph $G$. Then, from spectral graph theory, see~,  egin{equation} \label{th3.4} \lambda_{N}(L(G))\leq 2d_{\mbox{\scriptsize{max}}}(G) \end{equation} We now claim mss convergence for $\alpha=\alpha_{\mbox{\scriptsize mss}}$. From Lemma~ and~(),  egin{eqnarray} \label{th3.7} ho\left(W- rac{1}{N}Jight) & = & \max \left(\lambda_{2}(W),-\lambda_{N}(W)ight) \ 
onumber & = & \max \left(1-\alpha_{\mbox{\scriptsize mss}}\lambda_{2}(L), \alpha_{\mbox{\scriptsize mss}}\lambda_{N}(L)-1ight) \ 
onumber & = & 1-\alpha_{\mbox{\scriptsize mss}}\lambda_{2}(L) \end{eqnarray} where the last step follows from the fact that from eqn.~() and~()  egin{equation} \label{th3.100} 1-\alpha_{\mbox{\scriptsize mss}}\lambda_{2}(L)\geq 0\geq \alpha_{\mbox{\scriptsize mss}}\lambda_{N}(L)-1 \end{equation} Taking expectation on both sides of eqn.~(), and since $0<E[\lambda_2(L)] 2d_max$, we get  egin{eqnarray} \label{th3.8} C\left(\alpha,\overline{L}ight)&=&\mbox{E}\left[ho\left(W- rac{1}{N}Jight)ight]\ 
onumber &=&1-\alpha_{\mbox{\scriptsize mss}}\mbox{E}\left[\lambda_{2}(L)ight]\ 
onumber &<& 1 \end{eqnarray} mss convergence then follows from Theorem~. This proves the sufficiency part. The necessary condition follows from the fact that, if $\lambda_{2}\left(\overline{L}ight)=0$, Theorem~ precludes convergence of the mean vector. Since, by Corollary~, convergence of the mean is necessary for mss convergence, we conclude that, if $\lambda_{2}\left(\overline{L}ight)=0$, no choice of $\alpha$ will result in mss convergence. proof Theorem~ gives necessary and sufficient conditions on the probability distribution of the Laplacian $L$ for mean square convergence. This is significant as it relates mss convergence to the network topology. Because this condition is in terms of the algebraic connectivity of the mean Laplacian associated with the probability distribution of edge formation~$P$, it is straightforward to check. Almost Sure Convergence We extend the results of the earlier sections and show that $\lambda_{2}\left(\overline{L}ight)>0$ is also a necessary and sufficient condition for a.s.~convergence of the sequence $\left\{\mathbf{x}(i)ight\}_{i=0}^{\infty}$. Before proceeding to a formal statement and proof of this, we recall some basic facts about the convergence of (scalar) random variables. definition[A.S.~Convergence of random variables] Let $\left\{\mathbf{\xi}_{i}ight\}_{i=0}^{\infty}$ be a sequence of random variables defined on some common probability space $(\Omega,\mathcal{F},\mathbb{P})$. Then $\left\{\mathbf{\xi}_{i}ight\}_{i=0}^{\infty}$ converges a.s.~to another random variable $\mathbf{\xi}$ defined on $(\Omega,\mathcal{F},\mathbb{P})$ $(\mathbf{\xi}_{i}ightarrow\mathbf{\xi} \mbox{a.s.})$ if  egin{equation} \label{def:asconv1} \mathbb{P}\left(\omega\in\Omega ~:~ \mathbf{\xi}_{i}(\omega)\xrightarrow[iightarrow\infty]{}\mathbf{\xi}(\omega)ight) = 1 \end{equation} definition This definition readily extends to random vectors, where a.s.~convergence means a.s. ~convergence of each component (see~.) We also recall that mss convergence of a sequence of random variables $\left\{\mathbf{x}(i)ight\}_{i=0}^{\infty}$ implies convergence in probability through Chebyshev's inequality. Also, we note that convergence in probability implies a.s.~convergence of a subsequence (see~.) We now formalize the theorem for almost sure convergence of the state vector sequence $\left\{\mathbf{x}(i)ight\}_{i=0}^{\infty}$. theorem A necessary and sufficient condition for a.s.~convergence of the sequence $\left\{\mathbf{x}(i)ight\}_{i=0}^{\infty}$ is $\lambda_{2}\left(\overline{L}ight)>0$. In other words, if $\lambda_{2}\left(\overline{L}ight)>0$, then there exists an $\alpha$ such that $x(i)ightarrowx_avg a.s.$ On the contrary, if $\lambda_{2}\left(\overline{L}ight)=0$ then no choice of $\alpha$ leads to a.s.~convergence. theorem proof We prove the sufficiency part first. Like Theorem~ we give a constructive proof. We claim that the choice of $\alpha=\alpha_{\mbox{\scriptsize{mss}}}=1/2d_{\mbox{\scriptsize{max}}}$ (see eqn.()) leads to a.s.~convergence. To this end, define the sequence of random variables,  egin{equation} \label{th:as1} \mathbf{\xi}_{i} = \left\|\mathbf{x}(i)-\mathbf{x}_{\mbox{\scriptsize{avg}}}ight\|^{1/2} \end{equation} It follows from the properties of finite dimensional real number sequences (see~) that  egin{equation} \label{th:as2} \mathbf{x}(i)ightarrow\mathbf{x}_{\mbox{\scriptsize{avg}}}~ \mbox{a.s.}\Leftrightarrow\mathbf{\xi}_{i}ightarrow 0 ~\mbox{a.s.} \end{equation} From Theorem~ we note that  egin{equation} \label{th:as3} \mathbf{\xi}_{i}\xrightarrow{mss} 0 \end{equation} Thus $\mathbf{\xi}_{i}ightarrow 0$ in probability and there exists a subsequence $\left\{\mathbf{\xi}_{i_{k}}ight\}_{k=0}^{\infty}$ which converges to 0 a.s. Also we note from eqn.() that $0\leq\alpha_{\mbox{\scriptsize{mss}}}\leq 1$. Then, from eqn.(), it follows that  egin{equation} \label{th:as4} ho\left(W- rac{1}{N}Jight)\leq 1 \end{equation} Hence from Lemma~ we have  egin{eqnarray} \label{th:as5} \mathbf{\xi}_{i}^{2} & \leq & ho\left(W(i-1)- rac{1}{N}Jight)\mathbf{\xi}_{i-1}^{2}\ 
onumber & \leq & \mathbf{\xi}_{i-1}^{2} \end{eqnarray} Thus $\left\{\mathbf{\xi}_{i}ight\}_{i=0}^{\infty}$ is a non-increasing sequence of random variables, a subsequence of which converges a.s.~to 0. By the properties of real valued sequences $\mathbf{\xi}_{i}ightarrow 0 ~\mbox{a.s.}$ The sufficiency part then follows from~(). The necessary part is trivial, because $\lambda_{2}(\overline{L})=0$ implies that the network always separates into at least two components with zero probability of communication between them. Hence no weight assignment scheme can lead to a.s.~convergence. proof A note on Theorems~ and~: We consider only equal weights, i.e., all the link weights are assigned the same weight $\alpha$. However, it is interesting that, whatever the weights in particular, different weights for different links, a necessary condition for mss convergence (and a.s.~convergence) is $\lambda_{2}\left(\overline{L}ight)>0$. This is because (as argued in Theorem~) if $\lambda_{2}\left(\overline{L}ight)=0$, the network separates into two components with zero probability of communication between each other. Hence, no weight assignment can lead to mss~convergence. Thus, the necessary condition established in Theorems~ and~ for mss~convergence and a.s.~convergence respectively in the constant link weight case holds for the more general weight assignments also. In other words, if we have a weight assignment (with possibly different weights for different links) for which the consensus algorithm converges in mss (and a.s.), then we can always find a constant weight $\alpha$ for which the consensus algorithm converges in mss (and a.s.)

summary.content: The section discusses the convergence of average consensus in random topologies, focusing on the mean vector's convergence and the conditions required for it. It establishes that the mean state vector converges if the spectral radius condition \(\rho(\overline{W} - \frac{1}{N}J) < 1\) is satisfied, with necessary and sufficient conditions linked to the second smallest eigenvalue \(\lambda_2(\overline{L})\) of the Laplacian matrix. The section also introduces the mean convergence factor and identifies the optimal choice of the weight parameter \(\alpha\) that maximizes convergence speed, specifically \(\alpha^{\star} = \frac{2}{\lambda_2(\overline{L}) + \lambda_N(\overline{L})}\). Furthermore, it explores mean-square convergence, providing a sufficient condition for this type of convergence, which is dependent on the expected value of the convergence factor being less than one. The section concludes by establishing that mss convergence is achievable if \(\lambda_2(\overline{L}) > 0\) and suggests a specific choice for \(\alpha\) that ensures this convergence.

We study now the mss convergence of the algorithm through the convergence metrics given in Definitions~. In the sequel, whenever we refer to convergence rate of the algorithm, we mean the mss convergence gain per iteration, $S_{\mbox{\scriptsize{g}}}(\alpha,\overline{L})$, unless otherwise stated. We derive bounds on the mss convergence rate of the algorithm. We assume that $\lambda_{2}\left(\overline{L}ight)>0$. Hence, by Theorem~, there exists $\alpha$, in particular, $\alpha_{\mbox{\scriptsize mss}}$, leading to mss convergence. However, given a particular distribution of the Laplacian $L$, the actual choice of $\alpha$ plays a significant role in determining the convergence rate. Thus, given a particular distribution of $L$, we must choose that value of $\alpha$ that maximizes the convergence speed. From Theorem~, we note that, the smaller the mss-convergence factor $C\left(\alpha,\overline{L}ight)$ given by~() is, the faster the convergence is. For a given edge formation probability distribution~$P$ (and hence $\overline{L}$), the value of $C\left(\alpha,\overline{L}ight)$ depends on $\alpha$. Thus, to maximize convergence speed for a given $P$, we perform the minimization  egin{eqnarray} \label{min_conv_func} C^{\ast}\left(\overline{L}ight)& = & \min_{\alpha}~C(\alpha,\overline{L})\ 
onumber & = & \min_{\alpha}~\mbox{E}\left[ho\left(W- rac{1}{N}Jight)ight] \end{eqnarray} We present the results in terms of the best achievable mss convergence rate $S_{\mbox{\scriptsize{g}}}^{\ast}(\overline{L})$  egin{equation} %\label{def_Tc} T_{\mbox{\scriptsize{c}}}^{\ast} &=& - rac{1}{\ln %\left(C^{\ast}ight)}\  \label{def_Sc}  S_{\mbox{\scriptsize{g}}}^{\ast}(\overline{L}) =-\ln C^{\ast}(\overline{L}) %
onumber % &=&  rac{1}{T_{\mbox{\scriptsize{c}}}^{\ast}} \end{equation} The minimization in eqn.~() is difficult. It depends on the probability distribution of the Laplacian~$L$. But, by Lemma~, $C\left(\alpha,\overline{L}ight)$ is convex on~$\alpha$ for a given $\overline{L}$; so, its minimum is attainable using numerical procedures. In performing this minimization, we do not need to consider the entire real line for finding the optimal $\alpha$. The following Lemma provides a range where the optimal $\alpha$ lies. lemma Let $\lambda_{2}\left(\overline{L}ight)> 0$. Then  egin{equation} \label{l5.1} 0<\alpha^{\ast}< rac{2}{\lambda_{N}\left(\overline{L}ight)} \end{equation} lemma proof Since $\lambda_{2}\left(\overline{L}ight)>0$, by Theorem~, we can find $\alpha$ that leads to mss convergence. But, a necessary condition for mss convergence is convergence of the mean vector. From section~, the mean converges only if  egin{equation} \label{l5.2} 0<\alpha <  rac{2}{\lambda_{N}\left(\overline{L}ight)} \end{equation} Hence, the optimal $\alpha^{\ast}$ leading to fastest mss convergence must also belong to this range. proof We can bound the optimal mss convergence rate $S_{\mbox{\scriptsize{g}}}^{\ast}(\overline{L})$. lemma If $\lambda_{2}\left(\overline{L}ight)>0$, then  egin{equation} \label{Sc_lb} S_{\mbox{\scriptsize{g}}}^{\ast}(\overline{L})\geq\ln\left( rac{1}{1-\alpha_{\mbox{\scriptsize mss}} \mbox{E}\left[\lambda_{2}(L)ight]}ight) \end{equation} lemma proof By Theorem~, if $\lambda_{2}\left(\overline{L}ight)>0$, then $\alpha=\alpha_{\mbox{\scriptsize{mss}}}$ leads to mss convergence and  egin{eqnarray} \label{alpha_ms_conv_rate} C\left(\alpha_{\mbox{\scriptsize mss}},\overline{L}ight)&=&\mbox{E}\left[ho\left(W- rac{1}{N}Jight)ight]\ 
onumber &=& 1-\alpha_{\mbox{\scriptsize mss}}\mbox{E}\left[\lambda_{2}(L)ight]\ \label{calfacalfastar} &\geq& C^{\ast}\left(\overline{L}ight) \end{eqnarray} The Lemma then follows because  egin{eqnarray} \label{Sc_lbbb} S_{\mbox{\scriptsize{g}}}^{\ast}(\overline{L})&=&\ln\left( rac{1}{C^{\ast}\left(\overline{L}ight)}ight)\ \label{Sc_lbb}&\geq&\ln\left( rac{1}{C\left(\alpha_{\mbox{\scriptsize{mss}}},\overline{L}ight)}ight)\ \label{Sc_lb_rev}&=&\ln\left( rac{1}{1-\alpha_{\mbox{\scriptsize mss}} \mbox{E}\left[\lambda_{2}(L)ight]}ight) \end{eqnarray} proof

summary.content: The section investigates the mss convergence rate of the algorithm, defined as the mss convergence gain per iteration, \( S_{\mbox{\scriptsize{g}}}(\alpha,\overline{L}) \). It establishes that for \( \lambda_{2}(\overline{L}) > 0 \), there exists an optimal \( \alpha \), specifically \( \alpha_{\mbox{\scriptsize mss}} \), that ensures mss convergence, with the choice of \( \alpha \) significantly impacting the convergence rate. The section details a minimization problem to find the optimal \( \alpha \) that maximizes convergence speed, constrained within the range \( 0 < \alpha^{\ast} < \frac{2}{\lambda_{N}(\overline{L})} \). Additionally, it provides a lower bound for the optimal mss convergence rate, showing that \( S_{\mbox{\scriptsize{g}}}^{\ast}(\overline{L}) \) is at least \( \ln\left(\frac{1}{1-\alpha_{\mbox{\scriptsize mss}} \mbox{E}[\lambda_{2}(L)]}\right) \).

sections.section_title: Consensus With Communication Constraints: Topology Optimization
sections.content:
In the previous sections, we analyzed the impact of the probability distribution $D$ of the network topology on the mss convergence rate of the distributed average consensus algorithm. This section studies the problem of sensor network topology optimization for fast consensus in the presence of inter-sensor communication (or infrastructure) cost constraints. We assume equal link weights throughout. We consider $N$ sensors and a symmetric cost matrix $C$, where the entry $C_{nl}$ is the cost (communication or infrastructure) incurred per iteration when sensors $n$ and $l$ communicate. The goal is to design the connectivity graph that leads to the fastest convergence rate under a constraint on the total communication cost per iteration. Depending on the structure of the cost matrix $C$ and the network topology (deterministic or randomized), this optimization problem may have the following variants: - Fixed topology with equal costs: Here the entries $C_{nl}$ of the cost matrix $C$ are all equal and we look for the optimal fixed or deterministic topology leading to fastest convergence of the consensus algorithm. It is easy to see that the equal cost assumption translates into a constraint on the number of network links and the optimal solution is essentially the class of non-bipartite Ramanujan graphs (see~.) - Fixed topology with different costs (FCCC): In this case the inter-sensor costs $C_{nl}$ may be different, and we seek the optimal fixed or deterministic topology leading to fastest convergence. This is a difficult combinatorial optimization problem and there is no closed form solution in general. - Random topology with different costs (RCCC): This is the most general problem, where the costs $C_{nl}$ may be different and we look for the optimal (random or deterministic) topology leading to the fastest convergence rate under a communication cost constraint. Because the network is random, it makes sense to constrain the (network) average (expected) communication cost per iteration. Likewise, convergence should also be interpreted in a probabilistic sense, for example, the mean square convergence. To summarize, in the RCCC problem, we are concerned with: inparaenum[(i)] - designing the optimal probability of edge formation matrix $P$, - under an average communication cost constraint, - leading to the fastest mss convergence rate. inparaenum RCCC reduces to FCCC, if the entries of the optimal $P$ are 0 or 1. In this sense, the RCCC problem relaxes the difficult combinatorial FCCC problem and, as we will see later, will usually lead to better overall solutions, especially under medium to low communication cost constraints. This is because with a fixed topology, we are forced to use the same network always, while in the random topology case we can occasionally make use of very good networks, still satisfying the cost constraint. We can draw an analogy between RCCC and gossip algorithms (see~.) However the context and assumptions of the two problems are different. Reference~ optimizes the gossip probabilities for a given network topology under the gossip protocol---only two nodes, randomly selected with gossip probability, can communicate at each iteration--- and~ does not impose a communication cost constraint. In contrast, we design the optimal (equal) weight~$\alpha$ and the optimal~$P$ matrix leading to the fastest mss convergence rate, under an average cost constraint. The topology solution that we determine gives the percentage of time a link is to be used, or, as another interpretation, the probability of error asssociated with reliable communication in a given link. Because signal-to-noise ratio~(SNR) determines often the probability of error, enforcing the topology, i.e., $P$, is like selecting the SNR for each link. Random Topology with Communication Cost Constraints (RCCC) We are given $N$ sensors. We model the cost of communication by an $N	imes N$ matrix~$C=C^T$. The entry $C_{nl}\geq 0$, $n
eq l$, is the cost incurred by a single communication between nodes $n$ and $l$. Entry $C_{nl}=+\infty$ precludes sensors~$n$ and~$l$ from communicating. Let $P$ be the probability of edge formation matrix. The diagonal entries of $P$ are zero, although each node can access its data with zero cost. The $P$ matrix induces a probability distribution on the Laplacian $L(i)$, which at time~$i$ is a random instantiation based on the~$P$ matrix. The total cost incurred at stage $i$ is  egin{eqnarray} \label{cost_i} u(i)& =& - rac{1}{2}\sum_{n
eq l}L_{nl}(i)C_{nl}\ 
onumber & = &- rac{1}{2}\mbox{Tr}(CL(i)) \end{eqnarray} This follows from $C$ being symmetric with zero diagonal entries. Since $L(i)$ is a random matrix, the cost $u_{i}$ incurred at step $i$ is random. From~(), the expected cost incurred at step~$i$ is  egin{equation} \label{exp_cost}  orall i:\:\:\mbox{E}\left[u_{i}ight] %&=&\mbox{E}\left[- rac{1}{2}\mbox{Tr}(CL(i))ight]\ %
onumber & = &  - rac{1}{2}\mbox{Tr}\left(C\overline{L}ight) \end{equation} We consider the distributed averaging consensus model with equal link weights given in eqns.~() and~(). From Section~, mss convergence is determined by the convergence factor $C(,L)=E[ (W-1NJ)]$ or the convergence rate $S_{\mbox{\scriptsize{g}}}(\alpha,\overline{L})$ defined in~(). In particular, the smaller $C\left(\alpha,\overline{L}ight)$ (or larger $S_{\mbox{\scriptsize{g}}}(\alpha,\overline{L})$) is, the faster the convergence rate. The expected cost per iteration step in eqn.~() depends on~$\overline{L}$ and hence~$P$, which are in $1\leftrightarrow 1$ correspondence. Let $\mathcal{D}(U)$ be the set of feasible $\overline{L}$ (and hence~$P$) given a constraint~$U$ on the expected cost per step  egin{equation} \label{def_D} \mathcal{D}(U)=\left\{\overline{L}:- rac{1}{2}\mbox{Tr}\left(C\overline{L}ight)\leq Uight\} \end{equation} The RCCC problem can then be stated formally as: RCCC: Problem formulation.  egin{eqnarray} \label{eqn:rccc-1} % egin{array}{ll} %\max_{\alpha,\overline{L}} & S_{\mbox{\scriptsize{g}}}\left(\alpha,\overline{L}ight) \ %\mbox{subject to} %\end{array} \max_{\alpha,\overline{L}} ~S_{\mbox{\scriptsize{g}}}\left(\alpha,\overline{L}ight)\:\:\:\:\:\:\:\:\:\:\:\:\:\:\:\:\:\:\:\:\:\:\:\:&&\ 
onumber \mbox{subject to}\:\:\:\:\:\:\:\:\:\:\:\:\:\:\:\:\:\:\:\:\:\:\:\:\:\:\:\:\:\:  \overline{L}&=&\overline{L}^{T} \in\mathbb{R}^{N	imes N} \  
onumber  -1\leq &\overline{L}_{nl}&\leq 0,~n,l\in\{1,..,N\},n
eq l \

onumber  - rac{1}{2}\mbox{Tr}\left(C\overline{L}ight) &\leq& U \end{eqnarray} The second inequality constraint comes from the fact that $\overline{L}_{nl}=-P_{nl},~n
eq l$. The other inequalities follow from the properties of the Laplacian and the cost constraint. Alternate Randomized Consensus under Communication Cost Constraints (ARCCC) The RCCC problem in~() is very difficult to solve. We formulate an alternate randomized consensus under communication cost constraints~(ARCCC) problem. We show successively: inparaenum[(i)] - ARCCC is convex and can be solved by fast numerical optimization procedures; - ARCCC is a good approximation to~(); and - ARCCC leads to topologies with good convergence rates. inparaenum Point~(i) is in this section, while points~(ii) and~(iii) are studied in Section~ where we analyze the performance of ARCCC. onumber  -1\leq &\overline{L}_{nl}&\leq 0,~n,l\in\{1,..,N\},n
eq l \

summary.content: This section addresses the optimization of sensor network topology for rapid consensus under communication cost constraints, focusing on three variants: fixed topology with equal costs, fixed topology with different costs (FCCC), and random topology with different costs (RCCC). The RCCC problem aims to design a probability of edge formation matrix \( P \) that minimizes the expected communication cost while maximizing the convergence rate of the consensus algorithm. The expected cost per iteration is derived from the Laplacian matrix \( L(i) \) and the symmetric cost matrix \( C \). The section also introduces an alternate randomized consensus under communication cost constraints (ARCCC) problem, which is shown to be convex and solvable via numerical optimization, providing a good approximation to the RCCC problem and yielding effective topologies for consensus.

summary.content: In this section, the authors discuss the ARCCC topology optimization problem as an effective approximation of the original RCCC formulation. They establish bounds on the optimal value based on communication constraints and demonstrate through numerical studies that ARCCC topologies lead to fast convergence in distributed consensus. The analysis shows that replacing the maximization of the expected second eigenvalue with the second eigenvalue of the communication matrix simplifies the optimization process while maintaining performance. The numerical results indicate that higher values of the second eigenvalue correlate with improved convergence rates, confirming that ARCCC topologies are likely to perform well under the RCCC framework. Additionally, the concavity of the function relating the maximum eigenvalue to communication costs is established, providing insights into the performance bounds of ARCCC.

sections.content: The paper presents the design of the topology of a sensor network to maximize the convergence rate of the consensus algorithm as a convex optimization problem. We consider that the communication channels among sensors may fail at random times, that communication among sensors incurs a cost, and that there is an overall communication cost constraint in the network. We first establish necessary and sufficient conditions for mss convergence and a.s.~convergence in terms of the expected value of the algebraic connectivity of the random graph defining the network topology and in terms of the algebraic connectivity of the average topology. We apply semidefinite programming to solve numerically for the optimal topology design of the random network subject to the communication cost constraint. Because the topology is random, the solution to this optimization specifies for each realizable link its probability of error (aka, SNR), or the fraction of time the link is expected to be active. We show by a simulation study that the resulting topology design can improve by about 300~ common designs, e.g., geometric topologies where sensors communicate with sensors within a fixed distance. Our study also shows that the optimal random topology can achieve the convergence speed of a non-random network at a fraction of the cost. IEEEtran IEEEabrv,BibOptEqWeights document

summary.content: The paper formulates the topology design of a sensor network as a convex optimization problem aimed at maximizing the convergence rate of a consensus algorithm, considering random link failures and communication costs. It establishes necessary and sufficient conditions for mean square stability (mss) and almost sure (a.s.) convergence based on the expected algebraic connectivity of the network's random graph and its average topology. Utilizing semidefinite programming, the authors derive the optimal topology design while adhering to a communication cost constraint, specifying the probability of error for each link. Simulation results demonstrate that this optimal random topology significantly outperforms approximately 300 conventional designs, such as geometric topologies, achieving comparable convergence speeds at a reduced cost.
