Under the PC transform we replace an optimization problem over $X$ with one over ${\mathscr{Q}}$. As discussed at the beginning of Sec.~, the characteristics of the transformed objective can be very different from those of the original objective. Similarly, characteristics of any constraints on $X$ in the original problem can also change significantly under this transformation. More precisely, say we add to (P4) equality and inequality constraints restricting $x \in X$ to a feasible region. Then to satisfy those $X$-constraints we need to modify (P5) to ensure that the support of the solution $q_	heta(.)$ is a subset of the feasible region in $X$. This appendix considers some ways of modifying PC to do this. For earlier work on this topic in the context of delayed sampling, see~wost06,biwo04a,biwo04b,mawo05. Guaranteeing Constraints Say we have a set of equality and inequality constraints over $X$. Indicate the feasible region by a feasibility indicator function  egin{equation*} \Phi(x) = \left\{  egin{array}{ll} 1, & x 	extrm{ is feasible,}\ 0, & 	extrm{otherwise.} \end{array} ight. \end{equation*} For simplicity, we assume that for any $x$, we can evaluate $\Phi(x)$ essentially `for free'. The transformed version of this constrained optimization problem is  egin{equation*}  egin{array}{lll} (	extrm{P5}_c):& 	extrm{minimize}&\mathscr{F}_{\mathscr{G}}(q_{	heta}),\ &	extrm{subject to}&q_{	heta}(x)\Phi(x) = 0. \end{array} \end{equation*} We now present a parametrization for $q$ that ensures that it has zero support over infeasible $x$. First, let ${	ilde{q}}$ be any parametrized distribution over $X$, for instance, a mixture of Gaussians. Then using $\Phi(x \in X)$ as a `masking funtion' we parametrize $q_	heta(x)$ as  egin{eqnarray*} q_	heta(x) &	riangleq&  rac{{	ilde{q}}_	heta(x)\Phi(x)}{\int dx' \; {	ilde{q}}_	heta(x') \Phi(x')} 
onumber \ &	riangleq& {	ilde{q}}_{\Phi, 	heta}(x). \end{eqnarray*} This $q_	heta$ automatically meets the constraints; it places zero probability mass at infeasible $x$'s. It transforms the constrained problem (P5)$_c$ into the unconstrained problem  egin{equation*} (	extrm{P5}_{uc}): 	extrm{minimize } {\mathscr{F}}_{{\mathscr{G}}}({	ilde{q}}_{\Phi,	heta}). \end{equation*} Now consider the case where ${\mathscr{F}}_{{\mathscr{G}}}$ is an integral over $X$. Typically in this case we are only concerned with the values of the associated integrand at feasible $x$'s. For example, when $E_{q_	heta}(G)$ is of interest, it's usually because our ultimate goal is to find a feasible $x$ with as good a $G(x)$ as possible. In this situation it makes no sense to choose between two candidate $q_	heta$'s based on differences in (the $G$ values at) the regions of infeasible $x$ that they emphasize. More formally, our choice between them should be independent of their respective values of $\int dx \; [1 - \Phi(x)] q_	heta(x) G(x)$. We can enforce this by replacing the objective $E_q_(G) = dx q_(x) G(x)$ with $ dx (x) q_(x) G(x)$. If we then use the barrier function approach outlined above, our final objective becomes $qp$ KL distance with the integral restricted to feasible $x$'s. Generalizing this, when we are not interested in behavior at infeasible $x$ we can reduce the optimization problem further from (P5$_{uc}$), by restricting the integral to only run over feasible $x$'s. More precisely, write the original problem (P5$_c$) as the minimization of  egin{eqnarray*} \int dx [\int dg P(g \mid x, {\mathscr{G}}) ] F(g, q_	heta(x)) &	riangleq& \int dx \; \mu(x, q_	heta(x)) , \end{eqnarray*} subject to the constraints on the support of $q_	heta$. By using the ${	ilde{q}}$ construction we can replace this constrained optimization problem with the unconstrained problem  egin{eqnarray*} 	extrm{(A1): }{\mbox{argmin}}_{q} \; \int dx \; \Phi(x) \mu[x, q_	heta(x)] &=& {\mbox{argmin}}_{{	heta}} \int dx \;\Phi(x) \mu[x, {	ilde{q}}_{\Phi,	heta}(x)],\ &=& {\mbox{argmin}}_{{	heta}} \int dx \;\Phi(x) \mu[x,  rac{\Phi(x){	ilde{q}}(x)}{\int dx' \Phi(x') {	ilde{q}}(x')}]. \end{eqnarray*} As an example, say our original objective function is $pq$ KL distance. Define $Z^ eta_ dx p^(x) (x)$. Then our new optimization problem is to minimize over $$  egin{eqnarray*} {\mbox{KL}}(p^ eta_\Phi \; || \; {	ilde{q}}_{\Phi, 	heta}) &=& {\mbox{KL}}( rac{p^ eta \Phi}{Z^ eta_\Phi} \; || \; {	ilde{q}}_\Phi) 
onumber \ &=& -\int dx \;  rac{\Phi(x) p^ eta(x)}{Z^ eta_\Phi} {\mbox{ln}}[ rac{{{	ilde{q}}_	heta}(x)\Phi(x)}{\int dx' {{	ilde{q}}_	heta}(x') \Phi(x')}],
onumber\ &=& -\int dx \;  rac{\Phi(x) p^ eta(x)}{Z^ eta_\Phi} \; \{ {\mbox{ln}}[{{	ilde{q}}_	heta}(x)] + {\mbox{ln}}[\Phi(x)] - {\mbox{ln}}[\int dx' {{	ilde{q}}_	heta}(x') \Phi(x')]\}. \end{eqnarray*} The ${{	ilde{q}}_	heta}$ minimizing this is the same as the one that maximizes  egin{eqnarray}  \int dx  rac{\Phi(x) p^ eta(x)}{Z^ eta_\Phi} {\mbox{ln}}[{{	ilde{q}}_	heta}(x)] &-& {\mbox{ln}}[\int dx' \; {{	ilde{q}}_	heta}(x') \Phi(x')]. \label{eq:ensure_feas} \end{eqnarray} We can estimate $Z^ eta_\Phi$ using MC techniques. We can then apply MCO to estimate the $	heta$ that maximizes the integral differenceNote that in general this difference of integrals will not be convex in ${{	ilde{q}}_	heta}$ for product distributions, unlike KL$(p^ eta_ || q_)$. See the discussion at the end of Sec.~ on product distributions and $pq$ distance. in Eq.~. To generate a sample of sample $q_(x) = q_(x)(x)$ we can subsampleSay we want to sample a distribution $A(x) \propto B(x) C(x)$ where $B$ is a distribution and $C$ is non-negative definite, with $c$ some upper bound on $C$. To generate such a sample by `subsampling $B$ according to $C$' we first generate a random sample of $B(.)$, getting $x'$. We then toss a coin with bias $C(x') / c$. If that coin comes up heads, we keep $x'$ as our sample of $A$. Otherwise we repeat the process~[see][]wost06,roca04. ${	ilde{q}}_	heta$ according to $\Phi$. In some cases though, this can be very inefficient (that is, one may get many rejections before getting a feasible $x$). To deal with such cases, we can first run a density estimator on the samples of feasible $x$'s we have so far, getting a distribution $\pi$. (Note that no extra calls to the feasibility oracle are needed to do this.) Next write $q_(x) = (x) [q_(x) / (x)]$. This identity justifies the generation of samples of $q_	heta$ by first sampling $\pi(x)$ and then subsampling according to $q_	heta(x) / \pi(x) = {	ilde{q}}_	heta(x) \Phi(x) / \pi(x)$. In an obvious modification to the foregoing, we can replace the hard restriction that supp($q$) contain only feasible $x$'s, with a `soft' constraint that $q(x) infeasible x$. A similar alternative is to `soften' $(x)$ by replacing it with $\kappa$ for all infeasible $x$, for some $\kappa > 0$. For either alternative we anneal $\kappa$ down to 0, as usual, perhaps using cross-validation. Alternative ${\mathscr{F}}_{{\mathscr{G}}}$ Since we're maximizing our expression over ${{	ilde{q}}_	heta}$, the second, correcting integral in Eq.~ will tend to push ${{	ilde{q}}_	heta}$ to have probability mass $away$ from feasible regions. To understand this intuitively, say that ${{	ilde{q}}_	heta}$ is a Gaussian and that the feasible region is `spiky', resembling a multi-dimensional star-fish with a large central region and long, thin legs. For this situation, if we over-concentrate on keeping most of ${{	ilde{q}}_	heta}$'s mass restricted to feasible $x$, our Gaussian will be pushed away from any of the spikes of the feasible $x$'s, and concentrate on the center. If the solution to our original optimization problem is in one of those spikes, such over-concentration is a fatal flaw. The second integral in Eq.~ corrects for this potential problem. More broadly, consider typical case behavior when one applies some particular constrained optimization algorithm to any of the problems in a particular class of optimization problems. As a practical matter, there is a spectrum of such problem classes, indexed by how difficult it is just to find feasible solutions on typical problems of the class. On the one side of this spectrum are problem classes where it is exceedingly difficult to find such a solution, e.g., high-dimensional satisfiability problems with a performance measure $G$ superimposed to compare potential solutions. On the other end are ``simple'' problem classes where it is reasonable to expect to find a feasible solution. The `starfish' optimization problem is an example of a problem of the former type.Note that since we are discussing typical-case behavior, computational complexity considerations do not apply. For problems on the first side of the spectrum, where just getting a substantial amount of probability mass into the feasible region is very difficult, we may want to leave out the second integral in Eq.~. In other words, we may want to minimize KL$(p^ eta_\Phi \; || \; {	ilde{q}}_	heta)$ rather than KL$(p^ eta_\Phi \; || \; {	ilde{q}}_{\Phi,	heta})$. The reason to make this change is so that ${	ilde{q}}_	heta$ won't get pushed away from the feasible region. (As an aside, another potential benefit of this change is that if we make it, then for product distribution ${	ilde{q}}_	heta$, ${\mathscr{F}}_{{\mathscr{G}}}(.)$ is convex.) Even if we do make this change, when we sample the resultant ${	ilde{q}}_	heta$ we may not get a feasible $x$. If this happens, a natural approach is to repeatedly sample ${	ilde{q}}_	heta$ until we do get a feasible $x$. However the resultant distribution of $x$'s is the same as that formed by sampling ${	ilde{q}}_{\Phi,	heta}$ for the same $	heta$. So under this 'natural approach' we work to optimize a distribution (${	ilde{q}}_	heta$) different from the one we ultimately sample (${	ilde{q}}_{\Phi,	heta}$). This means that this approach may not properly balance our two conflicting needs for ${	ilde{q}}_	heta$: that it have most of its support in the feasible region, and that it be peaked about $x$'s with high $p^ eta(x)$. To illustrate this issue differently, take ${	ilde{q}}_{	heta}$ to be normalized, and to avoid multiplying and dividing by zero, modify $\Phi(x)$ to equal some very small non-zero value $\kappa$ for infeasible $x$ (as discussed above). Then under this `compound procedure', we ultimately sample ${	ilde{q}}_{\Phi,	heta}(.)$. However we do not choose ${\mathscr{F}}_{{\mathscr{G}}}({	ilde{q}}_{\Phi,	heta}) =$ KL$(p^ eta_\Phi \; || \; {	ilde{q}}_{\Phi,	heta})$ as the function of $	heta$ that we want to minimize. Instead we choose  egin{eqnarray} {\mathscr{F}}_{{\mathscr{G}}}( {	ilde{q}}_{\Phi,	heta}) &=& {\mbox{KL}}(p^ eta_\Phi \; || \;   {	ilde{q}}_{\Phi,	heta}) \;-\; {\mbox{ln}}[\int dx' \;  rac{ {	ilde{q}}_{\Phi,	heta}(x')}{ \Phi(x')}] . \end{eqnarray} Using Constraints for Unconstrained Optimization Return now to unconstrained optimization problems. Say that we have reason to expect that over a particular region $R$, the distribution $p^ eta(x)$ has values approximately $\kappa$ times as small as its value over $X \setminus R$. It would be nice to reflect this insight in our parametrization of $q$, that is, to parametrize $q$ in a way that makes it easy to match it to $p^ eta(x)$ accurately. We can do this using a binary-valued function $\Phi$ and the approaches presented above. To illustrate this, define ${	ilde{q}}_{\Phi,	heta}$ as above and choose the objective function ${\mathscr{F}}_{\mathscr{G}}(	heta) =$ KL$(p^ eta \;||\; {	ilde{q}}_{\Phi,	heta})$, where $(x) = $ over $R$, and equals 1 over $X R$.Note that we use $p^ eta$ in this ${\mathscr{F}}_{\mathscr{G}}$, not $p^ eta_\Phi$, which is what we used for constrained optimization. This is because our goal now is simply to find a $q_	heta$ that matches $p^ eta(x)$. There are no additional aspects to the problem involving feasibility regions that have no a priori relation to $G(x)$. Then working through the algebra, the $q_	heta$ that minimizes this objective is given by the ${{	ilde{q}}_	heta}$ that minimizes  egin{eqnarray} -\int dx p^ eta(x) {\mbox{ln}}[{{	ilde{q}}_	heta}(x)] \;+\; {\mbox{ln}}[\int dx' {{	ilde{q}}_	heta}(x') \Phi(x')] &=& {\mbox{KL}}(p^ eta \;||\; {{	ilde{q}}_	heta}) \;+\; {\mbox{ln}}[\int dx' {{	ilde{q}}_	heta}(x') \Phi(x')] 
onumber \ &=& {\mbox{KL}}(p^ eta \;||\; {{	ilde{q}}_	heta}) \;+\ 
onumber \ && \;\;\;\;\;{\mbox{ln}}[\int dx'_R \; \kappa {{	ilde{q}}_	heta}(x') + \int dx'_{X \setminus R} \; {{	ilde{q}}_	heta}(x')] . 
onumber \ && \end{eqnarray} The logarithm on the right-hand side is a `correction' to $pq$ distance from $p^ eta$ to ${{	ilde{q}}_	heta}$, a correction that pushes ${{	ilde{q}}_	heta}$ $away$ from regions where $\Phi(x) = 1$ (assuming $\kappa < 1$). To use immediate sampling with this parametrization scheme, once we find the ${{	ilde{q}}_	heta}$ that minimizes the sum of $pq$ distance plus that correction term, we would set $h$ to the distribution (proportional to) ${{	ilde{q}}_	heta}(x)\Phi(x)$. So we would generate our new samples from ${{	ilde{q}}_	heta}(x)\Phi(x)$, for example by subsampling.In practice, $\Phi(x)$ for this unconstrained case would not be provided by an oracle. Instead we would typically have to estimate it. We could do that for example by using a regression to form a fit to samples of $p^ eta(x)$ and then use that regression to define the region $R$.

summary.content: The section discusses the transformation of constrained optimization problems from the original space \(X\) to a transformed space \({\mathscr{Q}}\) using the PC transform, which alters both the objective and the constraints. To ensure that the solution \(q_\theta(.)\) adheres to the constraints of the original problem, a feasibility indicator function \(\Phi(x)\) is introduced, allowing for the parametrization of \(q_\theta(x)\) such that it has zero support over infeasible \(x\). The modified optimization problem is then expressed as an unconstrained problem, focusing on feasible regions, and the objective function can be adjusted to emphasize feasible \(x\) values. Additionally, the section explores methods for sampling from the distribution while maintaining feasibility, including the use of density estimators and soft constraints, and highlights the importance of balancing the support of \(q_\theta\) in feasible regions while optimizing the objective function.

Not all PC objectives can be cast as an integral transform. Properly speaking, the choice of objective should be set by how the final $q_	heta$ will be used. For instance, the concept of expected improvement suggested by ~moti78, and used by josc98, considers an objective (to be maximized) given by $\max(G_{\mathrm{bc}} - G(x), 0)$, where $G_{\mathrm{bc}}$ is the best of all the current samples, $\min_i \{G(x^i)\}$. This means that at each step we will take a single sample, and want to maximize the improvement. This is a simplification; even though the next sample may yield any improvement, it may be informative, so that we get a good sample ten steps later. A less simplistic objective is the following: In blackbox optimization, no matter how many calls to the (factual) oracle we make, we will ultimately choose the best $x$ (as far as the associated $G$ value is concerned) out of all the ones that were fed to the oracle during the course of the entire run. Our true goal in BO is to have the $G$ associated with $that$ best $x$ be as small as possible. For a discussion of distributions of extremal values, see ~[][]leli83,resn87. Given that $q_	heta$ varies over the run in a way that we do not know beforehand, how can one approximate this goal as minimizing an objective function that is well-defined at all points during the run? One way to do this is to assume that there is some integer $N$ such that, simultaneously, - It is likely that the best $x$ will be one of the final $N$ calls to the oracle during the run; - It is likely that $q_	heta$ will not vary much during the generation of those final $N$ samples. Under (2) we can approximate the $q_	heta$'s that are used to generate the final $N$ calls as all being equal to some canonical $q_	heta$. Under (1), our goal then becomes finding the canonical $q_	heta$ that, when sampled $N$ times, produces a set of $x$'s whose best element is as good as possible. An obvious variant of this reasoning is to have $N$ vary across the run of the entire algorithm, at any iteration $t$ being only the number of remaining calls to the oracle that we presume will be made. In this variant, one would modify the elite objective function to only involve the $N(t)$ remaining samples whose $G$ value is better than the best found by iteration $t$. For the case $N=1$, this is analogous to the expected improvement idea in~josc98. Note that this variant objective function will change during the run, which may cause stability problems. In this appendix we make some cursory comments about this objective function, which we call the elite objective function. We focus on the use of Bayesian FB techniques with this objective. For a noise-free oracle the CDF for the elite objective is  egin{eqnarray} {\mbox{CDF}}(k) &	riangleq& 1 - \int dx^1 \ldots dx^N \; \prod_{i=1}^N [q_	heta(x^i) \Theta(G(x^i) - k)]. \end{eqnarray} So the associated density function is  egin{eqnarray} f(k) &=&  rac{d \; {\mbox{CDF}}(k)}{dk} 
onumber \ &=& N q_	heta(k) [\int dx \; q_	heta(x) \Theta(G(x) - k)]^{(N-1)}. \end{eqnarray} The associated expectation value, $\int dk \; k f(k)$, is not linear in $q_	heta$. Writing it out, the posterior expected best-of-$K$ value returned by the oracle when queries are generated by sampling $q_	heta$ is  egin{eqnarray} \int dx^1 \ldots dx^K \; \prod_{i=1}^K q_	heta(x^i) \int dG \; P(G \mid D) \; \int dg^1 \ldots dg^K \prod_{j=1}^K P(g^k \mid x^k, G) {\mbox{min}}_k \{g^k\} \label{eq:elite} \end{eqnarray} We want the $	heta$ minimizing this. Say we knew the exact posterior $P(G \mid D)$ and could evaluate the associated integral in Eq.~ closed-form. In this case there would be need for the parametric machine learning techniques used in the text. In particular there would be no need for regularization --- an analogous role is played by the prior $P(G)$ underlying $P(G \mid D)$. When we cannot evaluate the integral in closed form we must approximate it. To illustrate this, as in Sec.~, for simplicity consider a single-valued oracle $G$. This reduces Eq.~ to  egin{eqnarray}  \int dx^1 \ldots dx^K \; \prod_{i=1}^K q_	heta(x^i) \int dG \;  P(G \mid D) {\mbox{min}}_k \{G(x^k)\}.  \label{eq:elite_single_valued}  \end{eqnarray} (The analogous FB MCO equation for objective functions involving a single integral Eq.~; here the single `$x$' in that equation is replaced with a set of $K$ $x$'s sampled from $q_{	heta}$.) To approximate this integral we draw $N_T$ sample-vectors of $K$ $x$'s each, using a sampling distribution $h_c(x)$ to do so. At the same time we draw $N_T$ fictitious oracles from some sampling distribution $H$ over oracles. To simplify notation, let ${\vec{x}}$ indicate such a $K$-tuple of $x$'s. (So for multidimensional $X$, ${\vec{x}}$ is actually a matrix.) Also write  egin{eqnarray} h_c({\vec{x}}) &	riangleq& \prod_{i=1}^K {h_c}(x^k), 
onumber \ q_	heta({\vec{x}}) &	riangleq& \prod_{i=1}^K q_	heta(x^k), 
onumber \ G({\vec{x}}) &	riangleq& (G(x^1), \ldots, G(x^K)).  \end{eqnarray} With this notation, the estimate based on fictitious samples introduced in Sec.~ becomesIn practice there might be more efficient sampling procedures than Eq.~. For example, one could form $NK$ samples of ${h_c}(x)$ and $N$ samples of $H(G)$, to get two sets, which one then subsamples many times, to get pairs $[{\vec{x}}, G({\vec{x}})]$.  egin{eqnarray} \sum_{i = 1}^N  \prod_{j=i}^K  rac{q_	heta(x^j_i)}{{h_c}(x^j_i)}  rac{P(G_i \mid D)}{H(G_i)} {\mbox{min}}_{k=1,\ldots K} \{G_i(x^k_i)\} . \label{eq:elite_sum} \end{eqnarray} As discussed in Sec.~, it is often good to set $H(G)$ to be as close to $P(G \mid D)$ as possible. So for example if we assume a Gaussian process model, typically we can set $H(G_i) = P(G_i D)$, and then directly sample $H$ to get the values of one $G_i$ at the $K$ separate points $x^j_i$. Alternatively, we can first form a fit $\phi(x)$ to the data in $D$. Next, for each of $N$ samples ${\vec{x}}_i$, sample a colored (correlated) noise process over the $K$ points \${\vec{x}}_i$\ to get $K$ real numbers. Finally, add those $K$ numbers to the corresponding values $\{\phi({\vec{x}}_i^j) : j = 1, \ldots, K\}$. This gives our desired sample of \$G_i({\vec{x}}_i)$\. To illustrate the foregoing, suppose $K = 1$, and that we have no regularization on $q_	heta$. Then, in general, the sum in Eq.~ is minimized by a $q_	heta$ that is a delta function about that data point $x^1_i$ with the best associated value $G_i(x^1_i) / {h_c}(x^1_i)$. However for $K > 1$, even without regularization, the optimal $q_	heta$ is not a delta function, in general.This suboptimality of a delta function $q_	heta$ is similar to the suboptimality of having all $K$ pulls in a multi-armed bandit problem be pulls of the same arm. In addition to the regularization-based argument in the text, this gives a more formal reason why the optimal $q_	heta$ should not be infinitely peaked. When $K > 1$, the peakedness of $q_	heta$ parallels the peakedness of another non-negative function over $x$'s, namely $P(G : G(x) is minimized at x D)$. However, if we run a few iterations of FB MCO with the elite objective, then $D$ grows, and so $P(G : G(x) is minimized at x D)$ gets increasingly peaked over $x$'s. (Intuitively, the larger $D$ is, the more confident we are about $G$, and consequently the more confident we are about what regions of $x$'s minimize $G$.) Accordingly, $q_	heta$ gets increasingly peaked as the algorithm progresses. Note that this happens even though there is no external annealing schedule. This reflects the fact that the elite objective has no hyperparameter or regularization parameter like the $ eta$ that appears in both the $pq$ and $qp$ objective functions.

summary.content: The section discusses the formulation of the elite objective function in the context of parametric learning and Monte Carlo optimization. It emphasizes that not all objective functions can be represented as integral transforms and that the choice of objective should align with the intended use of the final model \( q_\theta \). The elite objective function aims to maximize the improvement over the best current sample, considering the potential future value of samples. The section also introduces a method for approximating the objective function by assuming a fixed number of final oracle calls, allowing for the estimation of the best \( x \) based on a canonical \( q_\theta \). The mathematical formulations for the cumulative distribution function (CDF) and density function associated with the elite objective are provided, along with a discussion on the challenges of approximating the integral when the posterior distribution is not known in closed form.

One potential difficulty with this approach is that when descending $G_ eta(q)$ over $q$, one might encounter a $q$ such that the set argmax$_i$ KL$(p^ V_i || q)$ contains many constraints $i$. Now in such a case, since the overall problem is convex, we know that there is some direction $\delta q$ in which we could infinitesimally move $q$ that would lower all those (tight) constraints simultaneously. In other words, there is a $\delta q$ having non-zero dot product with the $q$-gradients of all the members of the set argmax$_i$ KL$(p^ V_i || q)$. Moreover, finding such a $ q$ is just a Linear Programming (LP) problem. In particular, we can use LP techniques to find the $\delta q$ that has minimal dot product with the $q$-gradient $ rac{\partial}{\partial q} {\mathbb{E}}_{q,{\mathscr{G}}}(g)$ while having non-zero dot product with the $q$-gradients of all the members of the set argmax$_i$ KL$(p^ eta V_i \;||\; q)$. Once we have solved for this $\delta q$, we could take a small step along it, and then again find the set argmax$_i$ KL$(p^ eta V_i \;||\; q)$ to continue the descent process.As an alternative, one could address the difficulty by temporarilly approximating $G_ eta(q)$, for example as $[\sum_i (KL(p^ V_i || q))^m]^1/m$ for a large $m$. *** $ $ ii) Constraint satisfaction $ $ DHW: The following won't work. The reason is that KL distance from $q$ to (the Boltzmann distribution for) any single $V_i$ will be minimized by having $q$ proportional to $V_i$. It can't be proportional to $V_i$ for all $V_i$ though. In fact, what we want is to have our objective function be minimized for $q$ a delta function about a feasible $x$. However the KL distance between any single $V_i$ and that delta-function $q_	heta$ is infinite (!). We will get a lower value of the objective function if $q_	heta$ ranges over $x$'s that disagree with at least some of the constraints. Consider using the approach of part (i) in the special case of constraint satisfaction problems, where $G(x)$ is constant and therefore irrelevant. In such problems, there is no issue of `balancing' the conflicting needs that ${	ilde{q}}_	heta$ have as much as possible of its probability mass on feasible $x$'s and that it be concentrated on $x$'s with large $p^ eta(x)$. So the modification discussed above in which one uses the objective function KL$(p^ eta_\Phi \; || \; {	ilde{q}}_	heta)$ rather than KL$(p^ eta_\Phi \; || \; {	ilde{q}}_{\Phi,	heta})$ is less problematic for constraint satisfication problems than for constrained optimization problems. In constraint satisfication that modification means using  egin{eqnarray} {\mbox{KL}}( rac{\Phi}{\int dx' \Phi(x')} \; || \; {	ilde{q}}_	heta) \end{eqnarray} rather than  egin{eqnarray} {\mbox{KL}}( rac{\Phi}{\int dx' \Phi(x')} \; || \;  rac{{	ilde{q}}_	heta}{\int dx' \; {{	ilde{q}}_	heta}(x') \Phi(x')}). \end{eqnarray} Under this modification we don't have the second integral of Eq.~ pushing ${	ilde{q}}_	heta$ away from feasible $x$'s. Due to this, the modification may outperform the original approach, as far as finding a feasible $x$ is concerned. Indeed, for this constraint satisfaction case, it makes sense to consider an objective given by a further slight modification,  egin{eqnarray} {\mathscr{F}}_\Phi(	heta) &	riangleq& {\mbox{KL}}( rac{e^{- eta [1  - \Phi]}}{\int dx' e^{- eta \Phi(x')}} \; || \; {{q}}_	heta) 
onumber \ &	riangleq& {\mbox{KL}}(ho^{ eta,\Phi} \; || \; {{q}}_	heta) \label{eq:constr_sat} \end{eqnarray} where since we are not using masking to parameterize $q$ there is no reason any more for a tilde over $q$. This ${\mathscr{F}}_\Phi$ is just $pq$ distance for a `$G(x)$' set equal to $1 - \Phi(x)$. So if we believe that in general PC using $pq$ distance will find a good solution to (P4), then we would expect that using it with the objective function in Eq.~ will result in a good solution to the problem of finding an $x$ that minimizes $1 - \Phi(x)$, that is, the problem of finding a feasible $x$. Now consider the particular case where the constraint function $\Phi$ is given by the intersection of $M$ constraints, where $M$ is very large. Say that each region in $X$ separately meeting one of the $M$ constraints is substantial, but due to the size of $M$, $\Phi(x) = 1$ only for an extremely small subregion of $X$. In such a situation, it may be that early in the run all sample $x$'s have $\Phi(x) = 0$. This would mean that those samples provide no information on how to modify $q_	heta$ to have it concentrate more on feasible $x$'s. Intuitively, one way around this problem would be somehow to decompose $\Phi$ into the $M$ constituent constraints, and address them separately and simultaneously. Since the feasible region for each separate constraint is large, even early in the run each of those constraints $separately$ would consider many sample $x$'s to be feasible. (The constraints would disagree though on which $x$'s they consider feasible.) So we might be able to Monte Carlo estimate feasibility information on the constraints taken separately. The goal would be to then combine such information from all the constraints, to solve our overall optimization problem involving all $M$ constraints. To illustrate how one might do this, return to the case where $X = \vartimes_j X_j$ and each component space $X_j$ is relatively small and finite (e.g., $X$ is a hypercube). Consider product distributions $q_	heta$ and for simplicity dispense with the subscript $	heta$, that is, use the trivial parametrization $	heta = \{q(x) : x \in X\}$. Write each of the $M$ constraints as a feasibility function $V_i(x)$ that equals 1 if constraint $i$ is satisfied, 0 otherwise. (So $\Phi(x) 	riangleq \prod_{i=1}^M V_i(x)$.) Also define  egin{eqnarray} G_ eta(q) &	riangleq& {\mbox{max}}_i [{\mbox{KL}}(ho^{ eta,V_i} \;||\; q)] . \end{eqnarray} For our product distribution $q$, each $KL(^, V_i || q)$ is a convex function of $q$. Therefore for fixed $$, $G_ eta(q)$ is a convex function of $q$. This means that there are no spurious local minima of $G_ eta$. Moreover, for any $ eta > 0$, the $q$ that minimizes $G_ eta(q)$ will have its support restricted to feasible $x$. So a natural iterative algorithm is to fix $ eta$, minimize the associated function $KL(^, V_i || q)$ as much as reasonable, and then raise $$ and repeat, as in conventional annealing. This approach can be used either for blackbox optimization or when we know the full optimization specification, so that there is no oracle. As an example of its application in the latter domain, consider a KSAT problem, where each clause of the problem corresponds to one $V_i$, and each $x_j$ is a single bit. Define $[^, V_i]^j$ as the marginalization of $^, V_i$ onto component $x_j$. For typical KSAT problems (that is, typical values of K) each such marginalization can be evaluated closed-form with little communication overhead. Now consider any term KL$(^, V_i || q)$ (one term for each clause $V_i$). That term will be given by a sum, over all components $x_j$ that occur in clause $i$, of KL$([ho^{ eta, V_i}]^j \;||\; q_j)$. (Those components of $x$ are the only ones on which $V_i(x)$ depends.) Again, for typical KSAT problems, for every clause $i$ there are few such $x_j$. That means that if in fact each $[ho^{ eta, V_i}]^j$ can be easily evaluated, then we can evaluate KL$(^, V_i || q)$ in closed form easily for any $q$, as well as its gradient, etc. Accordingly, we can optimize $G_ eta(q)$ in closed form, for example using epigraph methods. As another example of this approach, say that unlike the typical KSAT problem, we only have oracles for each $V_i$. So we have a blackbox constraint-satisfaction problem. For such a problem it may make sense to use immediate sampling to do the optimization. In this approach each term KL$(ho^{ eta, V_i} \;||\; q)$ is approximated as a sum, via importance sampling. (Note that one might to have a different sample of $x$'s for each $i$). One then does uses that sum to estimate the optimal $q$, in the usual immediate sampling ways. This max-based approach can also be helpful when $G(x)$ is not constant, so we don't have a constraint-satisfication problem. To see how, say that we ignore $G$ temporarilly, so that our constrained optimization problem becomes a constraint satisfication problem, with feasibility function $\Phi$. Run the max-based approach on this constraint satisfaction problem until we generate a solution $q_{	heta'}$ with small $pq$ distance to $ho^{ eta,\Phi}$ for a large $ eta$. Unlike the $q_	heta$ arising in the approach of part (i) of this appendix, $q_{	heta'}$ will in general not have its support restricted to $x$ such that $\Phi(x) = 1$. However it may well assign high probability to such $x$'s. If that is the case, then generating samples of ${	ilde{q}}_{\Phi,	heta}$ by subsampling $q_{	heta'}$ according to $\Phi$ should be relatively efficient (that is, should result in relatively few rejected samples). Accordingly, in running the constrained optimization approach of part (i), we may want to initialize ${{	ilde{q}}_	heta}$ to $q_{	heta'}$. *** $ $ ) Fictitous sampling for supervised learning $ $ In a fully Bayesian approach to the supervised-learning problem, the `target' stochastic process, which generated the training set $d$ of Eq.~, is not completely known. Accordingly, there is a distribution across all possible targets. That distribution reflects the information we have concerning the target, which includes in particular the fact that the training set $d$ was generated by sampling the target. This means that we should replace $P(y \mid x)$ in Eq.~ with a conditional distribution $P(y x,d)$. This gives the following optimization problem:  egin{eqnarray} {\mbox{argmin}}_	heta && \int dx \; P(x)[\int dy \; P(y \mid x, d) L(y, z_	heta(x))] . \end{eqnarray} To explicitly delineate the dependence on the target stochastic process on $d$, let $f$ indicate that target, and with some abuse of notation write the distribution of outputs $y$ for a given input $x$ and target $f$ as $P(y \mid x, f)$. With this notation our fully Bayesian treatment of supervised learning becomes the following optimization problem:  egin{eqnarray} {\mbox{argmin}}_	heta && \int dx \; P(x)[\int dy\,df \; P(f \mid d) P(y \mid x, f) L(y, z_	heta(x))] . \label{eq:bayes_sup_learn} \end{eqnarray} One can use importance-sampling MCO to do this minimization, as usual. To do this one first chooses a distribution $h_c(x)$ and $H(f)$. (For simplicity we assume that for any $x, f$, one can sample $P(y \mid x, f)$ directly.) Then one repeatedly samples $h, H$, and $P(y \mid x, f)$ to produce a set of triples, \$(x^i, y^i, f^i)$\. Using naive MCO, this transforms our supervised learning problem into  egin{eqnarray} {\mbox{argmin}}_	heta && \sum_i  rac{P(x^i) P(y^i \mid x^i, f^i) L(y^i, z_	heta(x^i))}{h_c(x_c^i)H(f^i)} \end{eqnarray} However for the usual reasons, unless the sample size is very large one would expect such a minimization to be a poor estimate of the $	heta$ solving Eq.~. The natural alternative to this naive MCO approach is to use PLMCO to solve for $	heta$. Note that that would mean using supervised learning to help a procedure for solving a supervised learning problem. $ $ ) Comparisons with Conventional Supervised Learning $ $ The immediate sampling algorithms explored in the text are indirect approaches for minimizing Eq.~. These indirect approaches are analogs of non-Bayesian approaches to supervised learning, in which one acknowledges that minimizing Eq.~ is the ultimate problem of interest, but one does not directly address that problem. Instead, one invokes bias-variance arguments, cross-validation, etc. In this appendix, we have proposed techniques to directly minimize the actual integral of interest, via importance sampling. Note though that in conventional Bayesian supervised learning, one is typically interested in `point predictions' of the value $z_	heta(x')$ for the $	heta$ minimizing Eq.~, for some particular $x'$. Usually, the minimization is over an extremely broad set of functions $\{z_	heta\}$, e.g., all twice-differentiable functions from $x$'s to $y$'s. These factors often mean that one never solves for the optimal $	heta$ (or the associated full function $z_	heta$) directly, but just for the value $z_	heta(x')$. This is what is done in Markov Chain Monte Carlo Bayesian methods, for example~. On the other hand, say one were interested in the optimal $	heta$ rather than a point prediction. For this case fictitious sampling (based on Markov samplers or importance samplers) using PLMCO rather than naive MCO would be a natural approach. *** $ $ ) Fictitious estimation for Monte Carlo $ $ Consider a simple Monte Carlo problem, of estimating the integral  egin{eqnarray} {\mathscr{F}}_{\mathscr{G}} &\equiv& \int dx dg \; P(g \mid x, {\mathscr{G}}) g  \end{eqnarray} for some potentially stochastic oracle $\mathscr{G}$. (This can be viewed as a degenerate case of the MCO problem where $	heta$ is fixed, so we have no optimization to do.) Say we do not know the oracle ${\mathscr{G}}$. However to help us estimate ${\mathscr{F}}_{\mathscr{G}}$ we have an information set ${D}$ that gives us information about the oracle. To fix the discussionm, we can assume that that information set contains samples of the oracle, as in conventional Monte Carlo estimation. Adopting the Bayesian decision theory approach, the information set induces a posterior distribution $P(F_G D)$. To use that distribution to estimate the integral we must specify an associated loss function $L$. Let ${\hat{\mathscr{F}}}_{\mathscr{G}}$ be our estimate of ${\mathscr{F}}_{\mathscr{G}}$. Then $L$ maps the pair $({\mathscr{F}}_{\mathscr{G}}, {\hat{\mathscr{F}}}_{\mathscr{G}})$ to an associated real-valued `loss'. That loss quantifies how good it is to make the estimate $ {\hat{\mathscr{F}}}_{\mathscr{G}}$ when the actual value is ${\mathscr{F}}_{\mathscr{G}}$. Our goal in Bayesian decision theory is to find the ${\hat{\mathscr{F}}}_{\mathscr{G}}$ that minimizes expected loss under the posterior $P({\mathscr{F}}_{\mathscr{G}} \mid {{D}})$ ~. Writing that out, Bayesian decision theory directs us to find the ${\hat{\mathscr{F}}}_{\mathscr{G}}$ that minimizes  egin{eqnarray} \int d{\mathscr{F}}_{\mathscr{G}} \; P({\mathscr{F}}_{\mathscr{G}} \mid {D}) L({\mathscr{F}}_{\mathscr{G}}, {\hat{\mathscr{F}}}_{\mathscr{G}}) \end{eqnarray} In particular, from now on we will assume a quandratic loss function. For this case our Bayes-optimal estimate of ${\mathscr{F}}_{\mathscr{G}}$ is just its posterior expected value,  egin{eqnarray} {\mathbb{E}}({\mathscr{F}}_{\mathscr{G}} \mid {D}) &=& \int d{\mathscr{G}}' \; P({\mathscr{G}}' \mid {D}) {\mathscr{F}}_{{\mathscr{G}}'} 
onumber \ &=& \int dx dg d{\mathscr{G}}' \; P({\mathscr{G}}' \mid {D}) P(g \mid x, {\mathscr{G}}') g . \end{eqnarray} For simplicity, from now on assume (${D}$ tells us that) the oracle is noise-free. So our posterior expected ${\mathscr{F}}_{\mathscr{G}}$ becomes  egin{eqnarray} \int dx dG' \; P(G' \mid {D}) G(x). \label{eq:mc_single} \end{eqnarray} By Bayes' rule, $P(G D) P(D G) P(G)$. Single-valuedness of $G$ implies that the likelihood $P(D G)$ (and hence $P(G D)$), can only have support on functions $G(x)$ that go through all the pairs $(x^i,g^i)$ in $D$. Single-valuedness also makes $P(D \mid G)$ the same delta function for all functions $G$ that are consistent with $D$, and therefore, it is only our prior over oracles, $P(G)$, that ranks these functions. In this way Eq.~ takes into account prior knowledge concerning $G$. This Bayesian approach also enables us to incorporate other information that we get from the factual oracle, for instance, gradients, uncertainty values, etc. Formally, all such information augments $D$, and therefore affects the $G$-dependence of the likelihood $P(D \mid G)$. If it cannot be evaluated closed form we can use MC to estimate the integral in Eq.~. One example of how to do that would be to use MCMC. An alternative is to use importance sampling. Note that in any such MC sampling, the $g$ values we generate are $not$ given by factual oracle $\mathscr{G}$. Rather they are given by counter-factual oracles ${\mathscr{G}}'$. To illustrate the foregoing, for simplicity assume that $D$ tells us that the oracle is noise-free. Then we can write  egin{eqnarray} {\mathbb{E}}({\mathscr{F}}_{\mathscr{G}} \mid {D}) \;\;=\; \; {\mathbb{E}}({\mathscr{F}}_{G} \mid {D}) &=& \int dG' \; P(G' \mid {D}) G'(x) 
onumber \ &=& \int dG'dx \; T(G') H(x)  rac{P(G' \mid {D}) G'(x)}{T(G')H(x)} . \end{eqnarray} To estimate this integral using importance sampling, we generate $N_T$ samples of $T$ and $N_H$ samples of $H$. This gives us a set of $N_H N_T$ values $G'(x)$. These are our fictitious samples. Our fictitious estimate of the integral is the average of those values,  egin{eqnarray} {	ilde{\mathscr{F}}}_{P(G \mid {D})} &\equiv& \sum_{i=1}^{N_T} \sum_{j=1}^{N_H}  rac{G^i(x^j)} {N_T N_H T(G^i)H(x^j)}. \label{eq:fict_est} \end{eqnarray} (Obvious variants of this approach don't evaluate all $N_T$ oracles $G^i$ at all $N_H$ points $x^j$.) *** Any such average is a high-dimensional integral. Moreover, typically it cannot be evaluated closed form.An important exception is that some Gaussian Process models with an appropriate covariance matrix can be evaluated closed-form. See~ and references therein. Sometimes one can use numerical expansions to approximate the integral over $U$'s (or $G$'s, as the case may be). For example, Laplace approximations can sometimes be used to do this~. In other cases though, it may make more sense to use MC sampling. *** Approximating the integral over $U$'s with such MC sampling introduces a second process of MC, subsequent to the one that generated $D$. That second MC process does $not$ involve calls to the actual oracle $U$. Instead it samples the distribution $P(U \mid D)$ to generate counter-factual $U$'s, and then samples those $U$'s. This gives us an additional set of samples beyond the original samples that were generated by calls to the true oracle. Intuitively speaking, we then combine those two sets of samples, and optimize $	heta$ for the resulting composite set. We use the term ficticious estimation to refer to such procedures, where one forms an estimate by combining an initial set of samples of a `true' data-generation mechanism with other samples that are generated subsequently to the original samples, and without again invoking the true data-generation mechanism. We use the terms ficticious samples and ficticious sampling to refer to that second set of samples and their generation, respectively. To distinguish it from the ficticious samples, we call a $D$ that was formed by importance sampling of the true oracle a set of factual samples. $ $ ) Ficticious estimation for MCO $ $ *** To perform a statistical analysis of any type of MCO requires that we first elaborate the statement that our `goal is to solve (P2)'~. We must specify exactly how happy we are for any pair (the value of the random variable, the output of our estimation algorithm). Formally, this is done with a function $L$ mapping the value of the variable whose value we do not know , together with the algorithm's output, to a real-valued `loss'. In MCO, the `algorithm's output' is a value for $\phi$, and the variable we do not know is $U$. So $L$ is a function of $U$ and $\phi$. *** As an example, say we have a function $G(x)$ that gives a `cost' for $x$. Then under distribution $q_	heta(x)$, expected cost is $ dx G(x) q_(x)$. summary.content: The section presents a Gaussian example for risk analysis, focusing on a two-dimensional Gaussian distribution $\pi$ characterized by its mean $\mu$ and standard deviations $\sigma_A$ and $\sigma_B$. The covariance matrix of $\pi$ has identical diagonal entries, leading to specific expressions for the off-diagonal entries and the probabilities associated with Monte Carlo Optimization (MCO). The difference in the loss function between two estimators, $\Delta L$, and the biases, $\Delta b$, are defined, revealing that the variances of the estimators are equal. The analysis shows that reducing the variance of either estimator decreases risk, while increasing their covariance also leads to a reduction in risk, highlighting the importance of variance and covariance in risk management within the context of MCO.

sections.content: Why should one do something like iterative focusing, or like setting the objective to $pq$ distance for a sequence of $\beta$'s? If we do follow an iterative procedure of this nature, how should we schedule the changes to our objective? To answer this, fix ${\mathscr{G}}$, and write the $qp$ distance from $q_\theta$ to the Boltzmann distribution at temperature $T$ as $qp_T(\theta)$. Say our ultimate objective is to minimize ${\mathbb{E}}_{q_\theta}(G)$. So $F(G, q_(x)) = G q_(x)$, that is, $E_q_(G) = qp$ distance for $T = 0$. For simplicity, assume $G$ is nowhere negative, that $h$ is uniform, and that $X$ is a compact subspace of a Euclidean space, with non-zero measure. Now one can form an IID sample of size $N$ from $h$, and then evaluate the associated importance-sampling empirical estimate of $qp_T(\theta)$ for every $\theta$. Label each of those estimates (one for each $\theta$, $T$ being fixed to 0) by ${\hat{qp}}_T(\theta)$. For each $\theta$, as one forms independent size $N$ samples of $h$, one induces a probability density function (pdf) over associated values of ${\hat{qp}}_T(\theta)$. Call that set of pdf's (one for each $\theta$) \$\pi_\theta({\hat{qp}}_T)$\. Since $qp$ distance is never negative, the support of each of those pdf's is the non-negative ordinate values, that is, each pdf `starts' at the origin (if not at a higher value). In an idealized version of each iteration of immediate sampling with $qp$ distance, we go through the following two-stage procedure: $ $ I) First we sample each pdf, getting associated values (one for each $\theta$) \${\hat{qp}}_T(\theta)$\. $ $ II) In the second stage we choose the $\theta$ with the minimal ${\hat{qp}}_T(\theta)$. $ $ Things are actually a bit more complicated, since the samples are correlated, but ignore that for now. Also ignore any quirks of getting caught in local minima in our EM algorithm (in which case we don't end up minimizing ${\hat{qp}}_T(\theta)$ over every possible $\theta$), etc. Also, in general one needs some tie-breaking scheme in (II). For now, ignore that as well. Consider the pdf's in the subset of the \$\pi_\theta({\hat{qp}}_T)$\ corresponding to delta function $q_\theta$'s. For $T=0$, almost all of these are candidates for the output of stage (II) of immediate sampling. This is because for almost all delta-function $\theta$, for our (fixed, finite) $N$ and uniform $h$, the pdf $\pi_\theta$ has almost all of its mass at 0 for $T=0$. As a result, almost all delta-function $\theta$ will result in ${\hat{qp}}_T(\theta) = 0$ --- and we know that no $\theta$ can result in a lower ${\hat{qp}}_T(\theta)$. Now since importance samples are unbiased, each pdf $\pi_\theta({\hat{qp}}_0)$ has as its mean the true $qp$ distance for that $\theta$ and $T=0$. Write that true distance as $qp_0(\theta)$. Since almost all the delta function pdf's have almost all their mass at 0, the fact that their means are non-zero implies that the widths of almost all delta function pdf's (that is, their variances) must be gargantuan. This means that at $T=0$, as one runs over the delta function $q_\theta$'s, there will be horrible correlation between the associated values of ${\hat{qp}}_T(\theta)$ (one for each $\theta$) and of $qp_T(\theta)$. (Almost all such $\theta$ will result in ${\hat{qp}}_T(\theta) = 0$, but their values of $qp_T(\theta)$ will vary considerably.) For tiny but non-zero $T$, there will be some variation in the values of ${\hat{qp}}_T(\theta)$ for the delta function $\theta$. Be we will still have a horrible correlation. This lack of correlation between what we minimize (${\hat{qp}}_T(\theta)$) and what we're interested in ($qp_T(\theta)$) means that we have no assurances that immediate sampling will do what we want. Note that this problem is almost absent in most parametric machine learning, being an artifact of how weird $F$ is (from the point of view parametric machine learning). Currently, to address this problem we use a non-uniform $h$. To choose that $h$ we start with a uniform $h$, and use non-zero $T$. Having $T > 0$ means that each pdf is shifted rightward by $-T S(q_) + ln(Z_T)$. The amount of shift varies from pdf to pdf, with the delta function pdf's shifting by just ln$(Z_T)$. Note that all other non-delta function pdf's are shifted rightward by less than this. Accordingly, it is now possible that random samples of those pdf's will be smaller values than random samples of the delta function pdf's. Due to this, the pdf's we will consider in stage (II) of immediate sampling will change from what they were for $T=0$. Depending on $T$, the pdf's that we consider will have relatively small variance (on the scale of the difference between their means), especially in comparison to the delta function pdf's. This means that there should be better correlation (as one varies $\theta$) between the smallest ${\hat{qp}}_T(\theta)$ values and the associated $qp(\theta)$ values in the pdf's that we will consider. We next use the $\theta$ minimizing ${\hat{qp}}_T(\theta)$ to set a new, non-uniform $h$. Then we repeat, with some scheme or other for shrinking $T$ as we do so. An alternative to this hack we currently use is to subtract a large enough constant from $G$ so that it is nowhere positive (assuming such a constant is finite). This means that every pdf now has support restricted to $non-positive$ ordinate values (as compared to the original scenario, where every pdf was restricted to positive values). Note though that the delta function pdf's still have the same (huge) density value at 0 as they did before. So samples ${\hat{qp}}_T(\theta)$ of those delta function pdf's are almost guaranteed to give higher values than samples for the other (non-delta function $\theta$) pdf's. This means that by searching for the $\theta$'s with smaller ${\hat{qp}}_T(\theta)$, we will $not$ be looking at the delta function pdf's. Instead we will be looking at pdf's with a far smaller variance. Those should have a relatively good correlation between ${\hat{qp}}_T(\theta)$ values and the associated $qp(\theta)$ values. All without any need to set a parameter like $T$. Cross-validation for automated annealing A variant of the procedure we use now exploits cross-validation to set $T$. To motivate this variant, note that our problem is that even though ${\hat{qp}}_T(\theta)$ is an unbiased estimate of $qp_T(\theta)$, it's variance for $T=0$ is so large that we can't use its value as a guide to set $\theta$. As we go from one $\theta$ to another, $qp_T(\theta)$ may change in ways completely at odds with how ${\hat{qp}}_T(\theta)$ changes, leading us badly astray in setting $\theta$. Everything else being equal, we want to search for $\theta$'s that minimize ${\hat{qp}}_T(\theta)$ over a set ${\mathscr{Q}}$ of $\theta$'s that have good correlation between ${\hat{qp}}_T(\theta)$ and $qp_T(\theta)$ (again, where `correlation' is as one varies over ${\mathscr{Q}}$). More precisely, for any $T$, we want such a good correlation over a set $U_T$ of $\theta$'s that have small associated ${\hat{qp}}_T(\theta)$ values, those being the $\theta$'s that our descent procedure will focus on. (The end of our procedure for implementing stage II of immediate sampling will, indirectly or otherwise, be a search over such a set $U_T$.) To formalize this, first recall that the expectation over sample sets $d$ of ${\hat{qp}}_{T,d}(\theta) = qp_{T}(\theta)$, since we're using an unbiased estimator, ${\hat{qp}}$. Let $P(\theta)$ be some distribution (e.g., uniform) over (the $\theta$ in) $U_T$. Define \begin{eqnarray} {\hat{qp}}_{T,d} &\triangleq& \int d \theta \; P(\theta) {\hat{qp}}_{T,d}(\theta). \end{eqnarray} Now consider the covariance \begin{eqnarray} {\mathbb{E}}_d \{ \int d \theta \; P(\theta) [{\hat{qp}}_{T,d}(\theta) - {\hat{qp}}_{T,d}]  \times [qp_{T}(\theta) - qp_T] \} \end{eqnarray} where $qp_T \equiv \int d \theta \; P(\theta) qp_{T}(\theta)$. This expectation is how well on average (over sample sets $d$), what we actually search on (values of ${\hat{qp}}_{T,d}(\theta)$ for $\theta$ chosen from $U_T$) covaries with what we're interested in (values of $qp_{T}(\theta)$). Since our estimator is unbiased, this expected covariance is just the variance of $qp_T(\theta)$ under $P(\theta)$. However for our purposes, we want to use unbiasedness differently, to expand the expected covariance as: \begin{eqnarray} {\mathbb{E}}_d \{ \int d \theta \; P(\theta) [{\hat{qp}}_{T,d}(\theta) - {\hat{qp}}_{T,d}]  \times [ {\mathbb{E}}_{d'} [{\hat{qp}}_{T,d'}(\theta) - {\hat{qp}}_{T,d'}]] \}. \end{eqnarray} This in turn just equals \begin{eqnarray} {\mathbb{E}}_d {\mathbb{E}}_{d'} \{ \int d \theta \; P(\theta) [{\hat{qp}}_{T,d}(\theta) - {\hat{qp}}_{T,d}]  \times [ {\hat{qp}}_{T,d'}(\theta) - {\hat{qp}}_{T,d'}] \}. \label{eq:cov} \end{eqnarray} More carefully, it isn't the expected covariance we're interested in, but rather the associated expected correlation, \begin{eqnarray} {\mathbb{E}}_d \{ \int d \theta \; P(\theta) [ \frac{ {\hat{qp}}_{T,d}(\theta) - {\hat{qp}}_{T,d}} { \sqrt{ {\mbox{Var}}[{\hat{qp}}_{T,d}]}} \times \frac{qp_{T}(\theta) - qp_T} { \sqrt{{\mbox{Var}}[{\hat{qp}}_{T}]}} ] \} \end{eqnarray} where the two denominator variances in the integrand are defined in the obvious way, in terms the associated numerators. As before, we can use the unbiasedness of our estimator to expand this expected correlation, getting \begin{eqnarray} {\mathbb{E}}_d {\mathbb{E}}_{d'} \{ \int d \theta \; P(\theta) [\frac{{\hat{qp}}_{T,d}(\theta) - {\hat{qp}}_{T,d}}{ \sqrt{{\mbox{Var}}[{\hat{qp}}_{T,d}] }} \times \frac{ {\hat{qp}}_{T,d'}(\theta) - {\hat{qp}}_{T,d'}} { \sqrt{{\mbox{Var}}[{\hat{qp}}_{T}]}}] \}. \label{eq:corr} \end{eqnarray} Note that the two denominator variances are different. As a crude approximation, one could just assume that Var$[{\hat{qp}}_{T,d}]$ does not change much as one varies $d$. In that case, up to the overall multiplicative factor $[{\mbox{Var}}[{\hat{qp}}_{T}]]^{-1}$, we can approximate Eq.~ with \begin{eqnarray}  {\mathbb{E}}_d {\mathbb{E}}_{d'} \{ \int d \theta \; P(\theta)   [{\hat{qp}}_{T,d}(\theta) - {\hat{qp}}_{T,d}] \times  [{\hat{qp}}_{T,d'}(\theta) - {\hat{qp}}_{T,d'}] \}. \label{eq:corr_approx} \end{eqnarray} We want the correlation of Eq.~ to be as high as possible, that is, we want to know what $T$ will cause that. So in the usual bootstrap way, for any given $T$ and sample set $d$, we can subsample $d$, and use those subsamples to estimate the expression in Eq.~ (or Eq.~). For any fixed $d$, we can estimate the correlation this way for many different $T$'s. We can then choose the $T$ that maximizes those subsample-based estimates of the expression in Eq.~. That $T$ is the one we would use to set the Boltzmann distribution $p_T$ in our $qp$ distance. As a crude example of this scheme, for each $\theta \in U_T$, we measure two values. The first is the value of ${\hat{qp}}_T(\theta)$ on a `held-in' subset of our sample (of $x$'s generated by IID sampling $h$). The second is the value of ${\hat{qp}}_T(\theta)$ on the held-out remainder of our sample. We then measure the correlation, across all the $\theta$'s in $U_T$, between the values of ${\hat{qp}}_T(\theta)$ in the held-in samples and the values in the held-out samples. To see why this makes sense, note that for $T=0$, $U_T$ will almost definitely consist of delta function $q_\theta$'s. So the correlation between the values of ${\hat{qp}}_T(\theta)$ in the held-in samples and the values in the held-out samples will be zero. For $T $, the $q_ U_T$ will all be close to uniform. I $suspect$ the correlation will again be small. For a sweet spot between these regimes, the correlation will be maximized. A probably preferable modification of this procedure replaces ${\hat{qp}}_T(\theta)$ as the value from the held-out sample with the empirical average $G$ as the value from the held-out sample (that is, it replaces it with `${\hat{qp}}_T(\theta)$' for zero $T$). In this variant one would find the $T$ that has a high correlation (over $\theta \in U_T$) between those empirical estimates of expected $G$ and the ${\hat{qp}}_T(\theta)$ values on the held-in points. The reasoning is that it is ${\mathbb{E}}_{q_\theta}(G)$ that we're ultimately interested in, and properly speaking, Eq.~ should be modified accordingly. Consider the `sweet spot' $T$ for this correlation between held-in sample values of ${\hat{qp}}_T(\theta)$ and held-out sample values of ${\mathbb{E}}_{q_\theta}(G)$. It is at this $T$ that minimizing ${\hat{qp}}_T(\theta)$ over all $U_T$ --- our immediate sampling procedure --- has the highest probability of minimizing (an unbiased estimate of) ${\mathbb{E}}_{q_\theta \in U_T}(G)$. As a practical matter, we may not want to just search for the $T$ that maximizes this correlation of the elements in the associated $U_T$. After all, one can imagine a situation where that correlation is high, but the associated (held-out sample estimate of) ${\mathbb{E}}_{q_\theta}(G)$ is poor. In such a case, for our best-correlating $T$, the ordering of the values ${\hat{qp}}_T(\theta)$ accurately tracks the ordering of associated values of ${\mathbb{E}}_{q_\theta}(G)$. However finding the $q_\theta \in U_T$ that minimizes ${\hat{qp}}_T(\theta)$ will not (likely) result in a good value of ${\mathbb{E}}_{q_\theta}(G)$. The problem is that while the correlation is high, $U_T$ consists only of poor $q_\theta$. So being able to reliably choose the best element of that $U_T$ isn't very helpful. As one way around this, for each $T$, form a regression. The independent variable in this regression is the held-in sample values of ${\hat{qp}}_T(\theta)$. The dependent variable is the associated held-out sample values of ${\mathbb{E}}_{q_\theta}(G)$. The `training set' for this regression is formed from the $\theta \in U_T$. Write this regression as the function $w(v)$ taking $R R$. Write the associated ($v$-varying) error bar of the regression as $\sigma(v)$. Finally, for any $T$, let ${\hat{\mbox{opt}}}(T)$ be the $\theta \in U_T$ that minimizes ${\hat{qp}}_T(\theta)$ (that is, that minimizes the independent variable of our regression) over the entire sample. Then it may make sense to use the $T$ that (to be conservative) minimizes $w({\hat{\mbox{opt}}}(T)) + \sigma({\hat{\mbox{opt}}}(T))$. This is our estimate of what an `unlucky' value of ${\mathbb{E}}_{q_{\hat{opt}}(T)}(G)$ would be, for using immediate sampling to pick a $\theta \in U_T$. In other words, it's our estimate of what ${\mathbb{E}}_q(G)$ would for an unlucky run of immediate sampling. There are obvious variants of all of this for $pq$ distance, etc.

summary.content: The section discusses the rationale behind using iterative focusing and the scheduling of objective changes in the context of minimizing the $qp$ distance from a Boltzmann distribution at temperature $T$. It introduces the concept of sampling from a probability density function (pdf) associated with the $qp$ distance estimates, highlighting the challenges posed by high variance in these estimates at $T=0$. The text emphasizes the importance of using a non-uniform distribution for $h$ and a non-zero temperature $T$ to improve the correlation between the minimized estimates and the true $qp$ distances. Additionally, it proposes a cross-validation approach to optimize the choice of $T$, aiming to enhance the correlation between the estimates across different sample sets, thereby improving the effectiveness of the optimization process.

sections.content: It is worth considering the conventional use of cross-validation to set a regularization parameter in parametertic parametric machine learning in light of the foregoing. Simplify such cross-validation into the following procedure: $ $ A) Form an $N$-element training set, $d_1$, by IID sampling $P(x) P(y \mid x)$, and find the $\theta$ that minimizes the associated value \begin{eqnarray} {\hat{\mbox{Tr-Err}}} (\theta) &\triangleq& \frac{\sum_i L^i_1(\theta) + T R(\theta)}{N} \end{eqnarray} where $T$ is the regularization parameter, $R$ is the regularizer, and the $L^i_1(\theta)$ are the $N$ functions from $\theta$ to ${\mathbb{R}}$ induced by evaluating $L(y, z_\theta(x))$ at the $x-y$ pairs in $D_1$. For use below, define $\theta(D_1, T)$ as that minimizing $\theta$. (This quantity is the parametric machine learning analogue of the quantity ${\hat{\mbox{opt}}}(T))$ discussed above.) $ $ B) Form an $N$-element training set, $d_2$, by IID sampling $P(x) P(y \mid x)$. Evaluate \begin{eqnarray} {\hat{\mbox{Gen-Err}}} (\theta) &\triangleq& \frac{\sum_i L^i_1(\theta)}{N} \end{eqnarray} for $\theta = \theta(D_1, T)$. $ $ ${\hat{\mbox{Gen-Err}}} (\theta(D_1, T))$ is an unbiased estimate of the value of the integral in Eq.~ evaluated for $ = (D_1, T)$. We do steps (A, B) for a set of several $T$, and then find the $T$ that minimizes $Gen-Err ((D_1, T))$. Our final fit is given by $z_(D_1, T)$ for that $T$. In light of our discussion on correlation in the preceding section, it is clear that there is a danger with this simplified version of cross-validation. While the estimates of the integral in Eq.~ given by $Gen-Err ((D_1, T))$ are all unbiased, they may have high variances. In such a scenario, using the $T$ that minimizes $Gen-Err ((D_1, T))$ may give poor results. To get around this, one might want to restrict attention to $T$ for which the associated variance of ${\hat{\mbox{Gen-Err}}} (\theta(D_1, T))$ is small. The problem is that it may be difficult even to ascertain whether the variance of ${\hat{\mbox{Gen-Err}}} (\theta(D_1, T))$ is small; one might not even know that one has a problem. One way to address that is to assume that the variance of ${\hat{\mbox{Gen-Err}}} (\theta)$ is a slowly varying function of ${\hat{\mbox{Tr-Err}}} (\theta)$. That way we can look at many $\theta$ such that ${\hat{\mbox{Tr-Err}}} (\theta)$ is close to ${\hat{\mbox{Tr-Err}}} (\theta(D_1, T)$ and see how much ${\hat{\mbox{Gen-Err}}} (\theta)$ `bounces around' across those neighboring $\theta$. This is what the idea of using a regression $w(v)$, recounted in the previous section, tries to do; $v$ is ${\hat{\mbox{Tr-Err}}} (\theta)$, and $w$ is $Gen-Err ()$. Indeed, even if the variance of ${\hat{\mbox{Gen-Err}}} (\theta)$ is fairly constant across the $T$ we're considering, it may make sense to use such a regression to estimate what $T$ would result in an optimal choice of $\theta(D_1, T)$. To see this, define $v^* Tr-Err ((D_1, T))$, and $w^* Gen-Err ((D_1, T))$. Then intuitively, with regression, for each $T$ one uses curve-fitting to combine the pair $(v^*, w^*)$ with neighboring $(v, w)$ pairs. That combination provides one's estimate of the full error integral for $v^*$, that is, for $\theta(D_1, T)$. In contrast, in conventional cross-validation, one ignores the information in those neighboring $v$'s, and just uses the value $w^*$ as one's estimate of the full error integral for $\theta(D_1, T)$. *** To that end, first note that the oracle is noise-free. This means that the posterior $P({G_c} \mid {{D}})$ only allows ${G_c}$'s that, if sampled at the $x$'s in ${{D}}$, would produce the associated $G(x)$ values found in ${{D}}$. In other words, if the fictitious sampling of $H$ produced the $x$'s in ${D}$, then the associated fictitious sampling of $T$ would have to result in the factual sample values $G(x)$ found in ${D}$. This suggests that the factual samples are in some sense consistent with fictitious sampling. To formalize this one might consider whether ${{\hat{\tilde}}{\mathscr{F}}}_{{D}}$ is an unbiased estimate of the Bayesian integral ${\mathbb{E}} ({\mathscr{F}}_{G_c} \mid {{D}})$. If it is, a natural idea for how to form our final estimate would be to use a weighted average of the fictitious and factual estimates, with the weights set using a bias-variance approach. One must be careful however. Strictly speaking there is no sense in which one can even ask if ${{\hat{\tilde}}{\mathscr{F}}}_{{D}}$ is an unbiased estimate of $E (F_G_c D)$, since that expectation value is only defined once ${D}$ is fixed. Similarly, there are two variances we can consider. One is a composite variance one could construct based on the point-variances Var$({G_c}(x^i_c) \mid {{D}})$, that is, based on the posterior variances of ${G_c}$ at the fictitious sample points. Another is the variance of ${{\hat{\tilde}}{\mathscr{F}}}_D(\theta)$ (as one varies ${D}$) as an estimator of ${\mathscr{F}}_G$. However these two variances have no direct relation to one another; they concern different underlying stochastic processes. As an alternative, one could ask what the relative weights of ${{\hat{\tilde}}{\mathscr{F}}}_{{D}}$ and $F_P(G_c D)$ should be when both are viewed as estimators of $\int dx \; G(x)$. In doing this one would consider how the outputs of those two estimators of $\int dx \; G(x)$ behave as one varies ${D}$ from one (factual) importance sample to another. ${{\hat{\tilde}}{\mathscr{F}}}_{{D}}$ is an unbiased estimator of $\int dx \; G(x)$. Its variance is trivial to estimate. To estimate the variance of ${{\hat{\tilde}}{\mathscr{F}}}_D(\theta)$, we could use the bootstrap. That would entail generating random subsets of ${{D}}$ with replacement, and then forming fictitious estimates of $\int dx \; G(x)$ for each of those subsets. Estimating the bias of $F_P(G_c D)$ is more problematic. The simplest approach would be to treat that bias as though it were the difference between ${{\hat{\tilde}}{\mathscr{F}}}_D(\theta)$ and ${{\hat{\tilde}}{\mathscr{F}}}_{{D}}$, for the purposes of calculating the averaging weights. However recall that in general the bias of Bayesian estimates is nonzero. So using a weighting of the two estimates based on bias-variance considerations, even in the limit of an infinite number of fictitious samples, where the fictitious estimate ${{\hat{\tilde}}{\mathscr{F}}}_D(\theta)$ exacty equals ${\mathbb{E}} ({\mathscr{F}}_{G_c} \mid {{D}})$, one would not use that FB estimate by itself. Rather one would average if with the factual estimate. This disagrees with the prescription of Bayesian decision theory. *** N.b., the GA-like view of the results of using xvalidation to dynamically adapt the number of mixing components: you're adding and removing species, as needed to speed the optimization. *** DHW, DEV: This section must ge fixed up. Shorten it to just have a copy of the abstract, and then a quick mention of other kinds of PL techniques we can test. One obvious way to apply PL techniques to blackbox optimization is to exploit parametric supervised learning to form a `fit' ${\hat{G}}_\theta(x)$ to the samples of the oracle. One then searches for the minimum of ${\hat{G}}_\theta(x)$. This allows the optimization to proceed with relatively few calls to the actual oracle. This approach is essentially what is done in Response Surface Methods (RSM)~. Note that this approach provides us with a new optimization problem over the same space $X$ as the original blackbox optimization problem. That new problem is in addition to the PL problem of finding $\theta$ from the samples. So this approach provides us with a succession of two search problems. Note also that this approach involves only a specific PL technique, namely the one used to do the supervised learning. In contrast, in this paper we do not consider how to apply some specific PL technique to design a new blackbox optimization algorithm. Rather we start with the blackbox optimization algorithm of immediate sampling. We establish that the search underlying immediate sampling is mathematically identical to the search underlying PL in its broadest sense. This identity reduces immediate sampling and its serach process in toto to PL and its search process. So to apply PL to blackbox optimization there is no need to add a subsequent search to the search of PL, e.g., a search over the fit ${\hat{G}}_\theta(x)$. The search of PL suffices.

summary.content: The section discusses the implications of conventional cross-validation for setting a regularization parameter in parametric machine learning. It outlines a simplified cross-validation procedure involving two steps: first, forming a training set and minimizing the training error with respect to the regularization parameter, and second, evaluating the generalization error for the minimized parameter. While the generalization error estimates are unbiased, they may exhibit high variance, which can lead to poor results when selecting the regularization parameter. To mitigate this issue, the authors suggest focusing on parameters with small associated variances and using regression techniques to estimate the optimal choice of the regularization parameter by considering neighboring values. The section also touches on the relationship between factual and fictitious sampling in estimating errors and the challenges of bias-variance trade-offs in Bayesian estimates.

paper.title: Calculating Valid Domains for BDD-Based Interactive Configuration
