paper.title: Epistemic Analysis of Strategic Games with Arbitrary Strategy Sets
paper.author: Krzysztof R. Apt

sections.content: Epistemic analysis of strategic games (in short, games) aims at predicting the choices of rational players in the presence of (partial or common) knowledge or belief of the behaviour of other players. Most often it focusses on the iterated elimination of never best responses (a notion termed as rationalizability), and the iterated elimination of strictly dominated strategies (IESDS). Starting with , and a large body of literature arose that investigates the epistemic foundations of rationalizability by modelling the reasoning employed by players in choosing their strategies. Such an analysis, based either on possibility correspondences and partition spaces, or Harsanyi type spaces, is limited either to finite or compact games with continuous payoffs, or to two-player games, see, e.g., or. In turn, in the case of IESDS the epistemic analysis has focussed on finite games (with an infinite hierarchy of beliefs) and strict dominance either by pure or by mixed strategies, see, e.g.. In this paper we provide an epistemic analysis of arbitrary strategic games based on the possibility correspondences. More specifically, denote by $\textbf{RAT}({\overline{\phi}})$ the property that each player $i$ uses a monotonic property $\phi_i$ to select his strategy (`each player $i$ is $\phi_i$-rational'). Then the following sets of strategy profiles coincide: - those that the players choose in the states in which $\textbf{RAT}({\overline{\phi}})$ is common knowledge, - those that the players choose in the states in which $\textbf{RAT}({\overline{\phi}})$ is true and is common belief, - those that remain after the iterated elimination of the strategies that are not $\phi_i$-optimal. This requires that transfinite iterations of the strategy elimination are allowed and covers the usual notion of rationalizability and a 'global' versionThe concepts of `global' and `local' versions are clarified in Section. of the iterated elimination of strictly dominated strategies. For the customary, `local' version of the iterated elimination of strictly dominated strategies (that is defined using a non-monotonic property) we justify the statement quote common knowledge of rationality implies that the players will choose only strategies that survive the iterated elimination of strictly dominated strategies quote for arbitrary games and transfinite iterations of the elimination process. Rationality refers here to the concept studied in. Our results complement the findings of in which transfinite ordinals are used in a study of limited rationality and , where a two-player game is constructed for which the $\omega_0$ (the first infinite ordinal) and $\omega_{0} + 1$ iterations of the rationalizability operator of differ. In turn, show that in general arbitrary ordinals are necessary in the epistemic analysis of strategic games based on the partition spaces. Further, as argued in , the notion of IESDS a la , when used for arbitrary games, also requires transfinite iterations of the underlying operator. The relevance of monotonicity in the context of epistemic analysis of finite strategic games has already been pointed out in , where the notions of strict dominance and rationalizability are studied using a public announcement logic.

summary.content: The epistemic analysis of strategic games focuses on predicting rational players' choices based on their knowledge or beliefs about others' behaviors, primarily through rationalizability and the iterated elimination of strictly dominated strategies (IESDS). This paper presents an epistemic analysis of arbitrary strategic games using possibility correspondences, establishing that the strategy profiles chosen by players under common knowledge of a monotonic property coincide with those selected under common belief and those remaining after iterated elimination of non-optimal strategies. The analysis allows for transfinite iterations, extending the usual notions of rationalizability and IESDS. Additionally, it highlights the necessity of transfinite ordinals in the epistemic analysis of strategic games, complementing previous findings on limited rationality and the implications of common knowledge of rationality. The relevance of monotonicity in finite strategic games is also discussed, linking it to public announcement logic.

sections.content: In this section we recall basic results concerning operators on a complete lattice and the relevant notions concerning strategic games. Operators Consider a fixed complete lattice $(D, \sse)$ with the largest element $\top$. In what follows we use ordinals and denote them by $\alpha, \beta, \gamma$. Given a, possibly transfinite, sequence $(G_{\alpha})_{\alpha < \gamma}$ of elements of $D$ we denote their join and meet respectively by $\bigcup_{\alpha < \gamma} G_{\alpha}$ and $\bigcap_{\alpha < \gamma} G_{\alpha}$. definition Let $T$ be an operator on $(D, \sse)$, i.e., $T: D \myra D$. - We call $T$ monotonic if for all $G_1, G_2$ \[ $G_1 \sse G_2$ implies $T(G_1) \sse T(G_2)$. \] - We call $T$ contracting if for all $G$ \[ T(G) G. \] - We say that an element $G$ is a fixpoint of $T$ if $G = T(G)$ and a post-fixpoint of $T$ if $G \sse T(G)$. - We define by transfinite induction a sequence of elements $T^{\alpha}$ of $D$, where $\alpha$ is an ordinal, as follows: - $T^{0} := \top$, - $T^{\alpha+1} := T(T^{\alpha})$, - for all limit ordinals $\beta$, $T^{\beta} := \bigcap_{\alpha < \beta} T^{\alpha}$. - We call the least $\alpha$ such that $T^{\alpha+1} = T^{\alpha}$ the closure ordinal of $T$ and denote it by $\alpha_T$. We call then $T^{\alpha_T}$ the outcome of (iterating) $T$ and write it alternatively as $T^{\infty}$. definition So an outcome is a fixpoint reached by a transfinite iteration that starts with the largest element. In general, the outcome of an operator does not need to exist but we have the following classic result due to .We use here its `dual' version in which the iterations start at the largest and not at the least element of a complete lattice. Tarski's Fixpoint Theorem Every monotonic operator $T$ on $(D, \sse)$ has an outcome, i.e., $T^{\infty}$ is well-defined. Moreover, \[ T^ = T = \G G T(G)\, \] where $\nu T$ is the largest fixpoint of $T$. 2mm In contrast, a contracting operator does not need to have a largest fixpoint. But we have the following obvious observation. note Every contracting operator $T$ on $(D, \sse)$ has an outcome, i.e., $T^{\infty}$ is well-defined. note In Section we shall need the following lemma. lemma Consider two operators $T_1$ and $T_2$ on $(D, \sse)$ such that - for all $G$, $T_1(G) \sse T_2(G)$, - $T_1$ is monotonic, - $T_2$ is contracting. Then $T_1^{\infty} \sse T_2^{\infty}$. lemma We first prove by transfinite induction that for all $\alpha$ \begin{equation} T_1^{\alpha} \sse T_2^{\alpha}.  \label{equ:inc} \end{equation} By the definition of the iterations we only need to consider the induction step for a successor ordinal. So suppose the claim holds for some $\alpha$. Then by the first two assumptions and the induction hypothesis we have the following string of inclusions and equalities: \[ T_1^ + 1 = T_1(T_1^) T_1(T_2^) T_2(T_2^) = T_2^ + 1. \] This shows that for all $\alpha$ () holds. By Tarski's Fixpoint Theorem and Note the outcomes of $T_1$ and $T_2$ exist, which implies the claim. Strategic games Given $n$ players ($n > 1$) by a strategic game (in short, a game) we mean a sequence $ (S_1, , S_n, p_1, , p_n), $ where for each $i \in [1..n]$ - $S_i$ is the non-empty set of strategies (sometimes called actions) available to player $i$, - $p_i$ is the payoff function for the player $i$, so $ p_i : S_1 S_n R, $ where $\cal{R}$ is the set of real numbers. We denote the strategies of player $i$ by $s_i$, possibly with some superscripts. Given $s \in S_1 \times \LL \times S_n$ we denote the $i$th element of $s$ by $s_i$, write sometimes $s$ as $(s_i, s_{-i})$, and use the following standard notation: - $s_{-i} := (s_1, \LL, s_{i-1}, s_{i+1}, \LL, s_n)$, - $S_{-i} := S_1 \times \LL \times S_{i-1} \times S_{i+1} \times \LL \times S_n$. Given a finite non-empty set $A$ we denote by $\Delta A$ the set of probability distributions over $A$ and call any element of $\Delta S_i$ a mixed strategy of player $i$. In what follows we assume an initial strategic game \[ H := (T_1, , T_n, p_1, , p_n). \] A restriction of $H$ is a sequence $(S_1, \LL, S_n)$ such that $S_i \sse T_i$ for $i \in [1..n]$. We identify the restriction $(T_1, \LL, T_n)$ with $H$. We shall focus on the complete lattice that consists of the set of all restrictions of the game $H$ ordered by the componentwise set inclusion: \[ $(S_1, \LL, S_n) \sse (S'_1, \LL, S'_n)$ iff $S_i \sse S'_i$ for all $i \in [1..n]$. \] So $H$ is the largest element in this lattice and $\bigcup_{\alpha < \gamma}$ and $\bigcap_{\alpha < \gamma}$ are the customary set-theoretic operations on the restrictions. Consider now a restriction $G := (S_1, \LL, S_n)$ of $H$ and two strategies $s_i, s'_i$ from $T_i$ (so not necessarily from $S_i$). We say that $s_i$ is strictly dominated on $G$ by $s'_i$ if \[ s_-i S_-i p_i(s'_i, s_-i) > p_i(s_i, s_-i), \] and write then $s'_i \succ_{G} s_i$. In the case of finite games, once the payoff function is extended in the expected way to mixed strategies, the relation $\succ_{G}$ between a mixed strategy and a pure strategy is defined in the same way. Further, given a restriction $G' := (S'_1, \LL, S'_n)$ of $H$, we say that the strategy $s_i$ from $T_i$ is a best response in $G'$ to some belief $\mu_i$ held in $G$ if \[ s'_i S'_i p_i(s_i, \mu_i) p_i(s'_i, \mu_i). \] A belief held in $G := (S_1, \LL, S_n)$ can be - a joint strategy of the opponents of player $i$ in $G$ (i.e., $s_{-i} \in S_{-i}$), - or, in the case the game is finite, a joint mixed strategy of the opponents of player $i$ (i.e., $(m_1, , m_i-1, m_i+1, , m_n)$, where $m_j S_j$ for all $j$), - or a correlated strategy of the opponents of player $i$ (i.e., $m \in \Delta S_{-i}$). Every joint mixed strategy of the opponents of player $i$ can be identified with their correlated strategy.

summary.content: This section discusses foundational concepts related to operators on complete lattices and strategic games. It defines operators, including monotonic and contracting types, and introduces the notion of fixpoints and outcomes through transfinite iterations. Tarski's Fixpoint Theorem is highlighted, establishing that every monotonic operator has a well-defined outcome, while contracting operators may not have a largest fixpoint. The section also outlines the structure of strategic games involving multiple players, detailing the components such as strategy sets and payoff functions, and introduces the concept of restrictions of games, which are subsets of the original strategy sets. Additionally, it defines dominance relations between strategies and best responses based on beliefs held in the game.

sections.content: The assumption that each player is rational is one of the basic stipulations within the framework of strategic games. However, rationality can be differently interpreted by different players.This matter is obfuscated by the fact that the etymologically related noun `rationalizability' stands by now for the concept introduced in and that refers to the outcome of iterated elimination of never best responses. This may for example mean that a player - does not choose a strategy strictly dominated by another pure/mixed strategy, - chooses only best replies to the (beliefs about the) strategies of the opponents. In this paper we are interested in analyzing situations in which each player pursues his own notion of rationality, more specifically the situations in which this information is common knowledge or common belief. As a special case we cover then the usually analyzed situation in which all players use the same notion of rationality. Given player $i$ in a strategic game $H := (T_1, , T_n, p_1, ,p_n)$ we formalize his notion of rationality as a property $\phi_i(s_i, G, G')$ that holds between a state $s_i \in T_i$ and restrictions $G$ and $G'$ of $H$. Intuitively, $\phi(s_i, G, G')$ holds if $s_i$ is an `optimal' strategy for player $i$ within the restriction $G$ in the context of $G'$, assuming that he uses the property $\phi$ to select optimal strategies. Here are some examples of the property $\phi$ which show that the abovementioned rationality notions can be formalized in a number of natural ways: - $\emph{sd}(s_i, G, G')$ that holds iff the strategy $s_i$ of player $i$ is not strictly dominated on $G$ by any strategy from the restriction $G' := (S'_1, \LL, S'_n)$ of $H$ (i.e., $ s'_i S'_i s'_i \succ_G s_i$), - (assuming $H$ is finite) $\emph{msd}(s_i, G, G')$ that holds iff the strategy $s_i$ of player $i$ is not strictly dominated on $G$ by any of its mixed strategy from the restriction $G' := (S'_1, , S'_n)$ of $H$, (i.e., $ m'_i S'_i m'_i \succ_G s_i$), - $\emph{br}(s_i, G, G')$ that holds iff the strategy $s_i$ of player $i$ is a best response in the restriction $G' := (S'_1, , S'_n)$ of $H$ to some belief $\mu_i$ held in $G$ (i.e., for some belief $\mu_i$ held in $G$, $ s'_i S'_i p_i(s_i, \mu_i) p_i(s'_i, \mu_i)$). Two natural possibilities for $G'$ are $G' = H$ or $G' = G$. We then abbreviate $\phi(s_i, G, H)$ to $\phi^{\: g}(s_i, G)$ and $(s_i, G, G)$ to $^ l(s_i, G)$ and henceforth focus on the binary properties $\phi(\cdot, \cdot)$. (The superscript `$g$' stands for 'global' and `$l$' for 'local'.) We say that the property $\phi(\cdot, \cdot)$ (used by player $i$) is monotonic if for all restrictions $G$ and $G'$ of $H$ and $s_i \in T_i$ \[ $G \sse G'$ and $\phi(s_i, G)$ implies $\phi(s_i, G')$. \] Each sequence of properties $\overline{\phi} := (\phi_1, \LL, \phi_n)$ determines an operator $T_{\overline{\phi}}$ on the restrictions of $H$ defined by \[ T_(G) := (S'_1, , S'_n), \] where $G := (S_1, \LL, S_n)$ and for all $i \in [1..n]$ \[ S'_i := \ s_i S_i \phi_i(s_i, G)\. \] Since $T_{\overline{\phi}}$ is contracting, by Note it has an outcome, i.e., $T_{\overline{\phi}}^{\infty}$ is well-defined. Moreover, if each $\phi_i$ is monotonic, then $T_{\overline{\phi}}$ is monotonic and by Tarski's Fixpoint Theorem its largest fixpoint $ T_$ exists and equals $T_^$. Intuitively, $T_{\overline{\phi}}(G)$ is the result of removing from $G$ all strategies that are not $\phi_i$-optimal. So the outcome of $T_{\overline{\phi}}$ is the result of the iterated elimination of strategies that for player $i$ are not $\phi_i$-optimal, where $i [1..n]$. When each property $\phi_i$ equals $\phi$, we write $T_{\phi}$ instead of $T_{\overline{\phi}}$. The natural examples of such an iterated elimination of strategies that were discussed in the literature are:The reader puzzled by the existence of multiple definitions for the apparently uniquely defined concepts is encouraged to consult. - iterated elimination of strategies that are strictly dominated by another strategy; This corresponds to the iterations of the $T_{\textit{sd}^{\: l}}$ operator in the case of ) and of the $T_sd^ g$ operator in the case of. - (for finite games) iterated elimination of strategies that are strictly dominated by a mixed strategy; This is the customary situation studied starting with that corresponds to the iterations of the $T_{\textit{msd}^{\: l}}$ operator. - iterated elimination of strategies that are never best responses to some belief; This corresponds to the iterations of the $T_{\textit{br}^{\: g}}$ operator in the case of and the $T_{\textit{br}^{\: l}}$ operator in the case of , in each case for an appropriate set of beliefs. Usually only the first $\omega_o$ iterations of the corresponding operator $T$ are considered, i.e., one studies $T^{\omega_0}$, that is $\bigcap_i< \omega_0 T^i$, and not $T^$. In the next section we assume that each player $i$ employs some property $\phi_i$ to select his strategies and analyze the situation in which this information is common knowledge. To determine which strategies are then selected by the players we shall use the $T_{\overline{\phi}}$ operator. We shall also explain why in general transfinite iterations are necessary.

summary.content: The section discusses the concept of rationality in strategic games, highlighting that players may interpret rationality differently. It introduces the notion of "rationalizability," which refers to the outcome of iterated elimination of strategies that are never best responses. The paper formalizes a player's notion of rationality as a property \(\phi_i(s_i, G, G')\), which indicates whether a strategy \(s_i\) is optimal under certain restrictions of the game. Various examples of properties are provided, such as \(\emph{sd}\) for strictly dominated strategies and \(\emph{br}\) for best responses, leading to the definition of an operator \(T_{\overline{\phi}}\) that iteratively eliminates non-optimal strategies. The section concludes by noting that the analysis will focus on the situation where each player's rationality is common knowledge, employing the \(T_{\overline{\phi}}\) operator to determine selected strategies.

sections.content: To proceed further we need to recall some basic facts concerning the epistemic analysis of strategic games. The approach taken below is based on the partition spaces, or more generally possibility correspondences. We follow here the exposition of. Given the initial game $H = (T_1, \LL, T_n, p_1, \LL,p_n)$ we assume a space $\Omega$ of states such that in each state $ $ each player $i$ chooses the strategy $s_i() T_i$. We assume that for $i \in [1..n]$ we have $|\Omega| \geq |T_i|$, where for a set $A$ we denote its cardinality by $|A|$. A natural example of $\Omega$ satisfying this assumption is the set of joint strategies in the game $H$. Then given a state $\omega := s$ we simply have $s_i(\omega) = s_i$. A possibility correspondence is a mapping from $\Omega$ to ${\cal P}(\Omega)$. We consider three properties of a possibility correspondence $P$: - for all $\omega$, $P(\omega) \neq \ES$, - for all $\omega$ and $\omega'$, $\omega' \in P(\omega)$ implies $P(\omega') = P(\omega)$, - for all $\omega$, $\omega \in P(\omega)$. If the possibility correspondence satisfies properties (i) and (ii), we call it a belief correspondence and if it satisfies properties (i)--(iii), we call it a knowledge correspondence.In the modal logic terminology a belief correspondence is a frame for the modal logic KD45 and a knowledge correspondence is a frame for the modal logic S5, see, e.g.. In the latter case the correspondence $P$ yields a partition $\{P(\omega) \mid \omega \in \Omega\}$ of $\Omega$. We assume that each player $i$ has a possibility correspondence $P_i$ on $\Omega$. Recall that an event is a subset of $\Omega$, and that an event $F$ is evident if for all $\omega \in F$ we have $P_i(\omega) \sse F$ for all $i \in [1..n]$. Following if each $P_i$ is a knowledge correspondence, we say that an event $E$ is a common knowledge in the state $\omega \in \Omega$ if for some evident event $F$ we have $ F E$. We write then $ K^* E$. Finally, (using a characterization of ) if each $P_i$ is a belief correspondence, we say that an event $E$ is a common belief in the state $\omega \in \Omega$ if for some evident event $F$ we have $\omega \in F \sse B E$, where $B E = \ i [1..n] P_i() E\$. We write then $ B^* E$. Each event $E$ determines a restriction $G_E$ of $H$ defined by $G_E := (S_1, \LL, S_n)$, where for all $j \in [1..n]$ \[ S_j := \s_j(') ' E\. \] In particular, when player $i$ knows (respectively, believes) that the state is in $P_i(\omega)$, the restriction $G_{P_i(\omega)}$ represents his knowledge (respectively, his belief) about the players' strategies. Given now a property $\phi_i(\cdot, G)$ that player $i$ uses to select his strategies in the restriction $G$ of $H$, we say that player $i$ is $\phi_i$-rational in the state $\omega$ if $\phi_i(s_{i}(\omega), G_{P_i(\omega)})$ holds. Intuitively, if the state of the world is $\omega$, player $i$ only knows (respectively, believes) that the state of the world is in $P_i(\omega)$. So $G_{P_i(\omega)}$ is the game he knows (respectively, believes in). Hence $\phi_i(s_i(), G_P_i())$ captures the idea that if player $i$ uses $\phi_i(\cdot, \cdot)$ to select his optimal strategy in the game he is `aware of', then in the state $\omega$ he indeed acts 'rationally'. We are interested in the strategies selected by each player in the states in which it is common knowledge (or true and common belief) that each player $i$ is $\phi_i$-rational. To this end we introduce the following set of states$\textbf{RAT}({\overline{\phi}})$ is always used in the context of specific possibility correspondences.: \[ $\textbf{RAT}({\overline{\phi}}) := \{\omega \in \Omega \mid $ each player $i$ is $\phi_i$-rational in $\omega$\ \] and focus on the following two sets of states: tabbing $CK({\overline{\phi}}) := \{\omega \in \Omega \mid $ \= for some knowledge \> correspondences $P_1, \LL, P_n$ \> $\omega \in K^* \textbf{RAT}({\overline{\phi}})$\, tabbing tabbing $CB({\overline{\phi}}) := \{\omega \in \Omega \mid $ \= for some belief \> correspondences $P_1, \LL, P_n$ \> $\omega \in \textbf{RAT}({\overline{\phi}})$ and $\omega \in B^* \textbf{RAT}({\overline{\phi}})$\ tabbing and the corresponding restrictions $G_{CK({\overline{\phi}})}$ and $G_{CB({\overline{\phi}})}$ of $H$. The following result then characterizes for arbitrary strategic games the restrictions $G_{CK({\overline{\phi}})}$ and $G_{CB({\overline{\phi}})}$ in terms of the operator $T_{\overline{\phi}}$. theorem Suppose that each property $\phi_i$ is monotonic. Then \[ G_CK() = G_CB() = T_^. \] theorem We prove three inclusions. (i) $G_{CK(\overline{\phi})} \sse G_{CB(\overline{\phi})}$. This inclusion (for an arbitrary $\overline{\phi}$) is an immediate consequence of the following alternative characterization of common knowledge due to : if each $P_i$ is a knowledge correspondence, an event $E$ is a common knowledge in the state $\omega \in \Omega$ if for some evident event $F$ we have $\omega \in F \sse K E$, where $K E = \ i [1..n] P_i() E\$. (ii) $G_{CB(\overline{\phi})} \sse T_{\overline{\phi}}^{\infty}$. Take a strategy $s_i$ that is an element of the $i$th component of $G_{CB(\overline{\phi})}$. So $s_i = s_i(\omega)$ for some $\omega \in {CB(\overline{\phi})}$. Then $\omega \in \textbf{RAT}({\overline{\phi}})$ and $\omega \in B^* \textbf{RAT}({\overline{\phi}})$. The latter implies that for some evident event $F$ \begin{equation}  \label{equ:F} \omega \in F \sse \{\omega' \in \Omega \mid \fa i \in [1..n] \: P_i(\omega') \sse \textbf{RAT}({\overline{\phi}})\}.  \end{equation} Take now an arbitrary $\omega' \in F \cap \textbf{RAT}({\overline{\phi}})$ and $i \in [1..n]$. Since $\omega' \in \textbf{RAT}({\overline{\phi}})$, player $i$ is $\phi_i$-rational in $\omega'$, i.e., $\phi_i(s_i(\omega'), G_{P_i(\omega')})$ holds. But $F$ is evident, so $P_i(\omega') \sse F$. Moreover by () $P_i(\omega') \sse \textbf{RAT}({\overline{\phi}})$, so $P_i(\omega') \sse F \cap \textbf{RAT}({\overline{\phi}})$. Hence $G_{P_i(\omega')} \sse G_{F \cap \textbf{RAT}({\overline{\phi}})}$ and by the monotonicity of $\phi_i$ we conclude that $\phi_i(s_i(\omega'), G_{F \cap \textbf{RAT}({\overline{\phi}})})$ holds. By the definition of $T_{\overline{\phi}}$ this means that $G_{F \cap \textbf{RAT}({\overline{\phi}})} \sse T_{\overline{\phi}}(G_{\textbf{RAT}({\overline{\phi}})})$, i.e. that $G_{F \cap \textbf{RAT}({\overline{\phi}})}$ is a post-fixpoint of $T_{\overline{\phi}}$. Hence by Tarski's Fixpoint Theorem $G_{F \cap \textbf{RAT}({\overline{\phi}})} \sse T_{\overline{\phi}}^{\infty}$. But $s_i = s_i(\omega)$ and $\omega \in F \cap {\textbf{RAT}({\overline{\phi}})}$, so we conclude by the above inclusion that $s_i$ is an element of the $i$th component of $T_{\overline{\phi}}^{\infty}$. This proves $G_{CB(\overline{\phi})} \sse T_{\overline{\phi}}^{\infty}$. (iii) $T_{\overline{\phi}}^{\infty} \sse G_{CK(\overline{\phi})}$. Recall that $H = (T_1, \LL, T_n, p_1, \LL, p_n)$. We first define - the functions $s_1:\Omega \myra T_1, \LL, s_n:\Omega \myra T_n$, - an event $E$, - the knowledge correspondences $P_1, \LL, P_n$. Suppose $T^{\infty}_{\overline{\phi}} = (S_1, \LL, S_n)$. Choose $j [1..n]$ such that the set $S_j_0$ has the largest cardinality among the sets $S_1, \LL, S_n$. Define the function $s_{j_0}:\Omega \myra T_{j_0}$ arbitrarily, but so that it is onto (note that this is possible since by assumption $|\Omega| \geq |T_{j_0}|$) and let $E := s^-1_j_0(S_j_0)$. Our aim is to ensure that \[ G_E = T_^. \] So we define each function $s_k: \Omega \myra T_k$, where $k \neq j_0$, in such a way that $s^{-1}_{k}(S_{k}) = E$. Note that this is possible since $|E| \geq |S_{j_0}| \geq |S_k|$. Next, we define each knowledge correspondence $P_i$ arbitrarily but so that for all $\omega \in E$ we have $P_i() = E$. Then for all $i [1..n]$ \[ G_P_i() = G_E. \] We now show that for all $\omega \in E$ each player $i$ is $\phi_i$-rational in $\omega$. So take an arbitrary $\omega \in E$ and $i \in [1..n]$. By the definition of the function $s_i(\cdot)$ a strategy $s_i \in S_i$ exists such that $s_i = s_i(\omega)$. Now, $T_{\overline{\phi}}^{\infty}$ is a fixpoint of $T_{\overline{\phi}}$, so $\phi_i(s_i, T_{\overline{\phi}}^{\infty})$ holds. But $T_{\overline{\phi}}^{\infty} = G_E = G_{P_i(\omega)}$, so $\phi_i(s_i(\omega), G_{P_i(\omega)})$ holds, i.e. player $i$ is indeed $\phi_i$-rational in $\omega$. To complete the proof take now an arbitrary strategy $s_i \in S_i$. By the definition of the function $s_i(\cdot)$ a state $\omega \in E$ exists such that $s_i = s_i(\omega)$. Further, we just showed that each player $j$ is $\phi_j$-rational in $\omega$. But by the definition of the knowledge correspondences $E$ is an evident event, so it is common knowledge in $\omega$ that each player $j$ is $\phi_j$-rational in $\omega$. Hence $\omega \in CK(\overline{\phi})$ and consequently $s_i$ is an element of the $i$th component of $G_{CK(\overline{\phi})}$. This proves that $T_{\overline{\phi}}^{\infty} \sse G_{CK(\overline{\phi})}$. This theorem shows that when each property $\phi_i$ is monotonic, the strategy profiles that the players choose in the states in which it is common knowledge that each player $i$ is $\phi_i$-rational (or in which each player $i$ is $\phi_i$-rational and it is common belief that each player $i$ is $\phi_i$-rational), are exactly those that remain after the iterated elimination of the strategies that are not $\phi_i$-optimal. It generalizes corresponding results established for finite strategic games (for their survey see ) to the case of arbitrary strategic games and arbitrary monotonic properties $\phi_i$. In , and examples are provided showing that for the properties of strict dominance (namely $\textit{sd}^{\: g}$) and best response (namely $\textit{br}^{\: g}$) in general transfinite iterations (i.e., iterations beyond $\omega_0$) of the corresponding operator are necessary to reach the outcome. So to achieve equalities in the above theorem transfinite iterations of the $T_{\overline{\phi}}$ operator are necessary. By instantiating $\phi_i$s to specific properties we get instances of the above result that relate to specific definitions of rationality. Before we do this we establish another result that will apply to another class of properties $\phi_i$. Consider the following natural property of the underlying functions $s_i(\cdot)$s: description - [A] For each strategy $s_i$ from $H$ a state $ $ exists such that $s_i = s_i()$. description theorem Suppose that property A holds and \begin{equation}  \label{equ:1} \mbox{$\phi_i(s_i, (\C{s_1}, \LL, \C{s_n}))$ for all $i \in [1..n]$ and $s_i \in T_i$.}  \end{equation} Then \[ G_CK() = G_CB() = H. \] theorem As noted in the proof of Theorem , for all $\overline{\phi}$ we have $G_{CK(\overline{\phi})} \sse G_{CB(\overline{\phi})}$. So it suffices to prove that $H \sse G_{CK(\phi)}$. So take a strategy $s_i$ of player $i$ in $H$. By property A a state $\omega$ exists such that $s_i = s_i(\omega)$. Choose for each player $j$ a knowledge correspondence $P_j$ such that $P_j(\omega) = \C{\omega}$. Then \[ G_P_j() = (s_1(), , s_n()) \] and, on the account of (), each player $j$ is $\phi_j$-rational in $\omega$. By the choice of the knowledge correspondences $\C{\omega}$ is an evident event. Hence it is common knowledge in $\omega$ that each player $j$ is $\phi_j$-rational in $\omega$. So by definition $s_i$ is an element of the $i$th component of $CK_{\phi}$. Note that any property $\phi_i$ that satisfies () and is not trivial (that is, for some strategy $s_i$, $\phi_i(s_i, H)$ does not hold) is not monotonic.

summary.content: The section discusses the epistemic analysis of strategic games using partition spaces and possibility correspondences. It defines key concepts such as belief and knowledge correspondences, which are characterized by specific properties. Theorems are presented that relate the restrictions of the game under common knowledge and common belief to the operator \( T_{\overline{\phi}} \), showing that if each property \( \phi_i \) is monotonic, then the strategy profiles chosen in states of common knowledge or common belief correspond to those remaining after iterated elimination of non-optimal strategies. Additionally, a theorem is provided that states if a certain property holds, then the restrictions equal the original game, indicating that under specific conditions, all strategies are rational.

sections.content: Let us analyze now the consequences of the above two theorems. Consider first Theorem. The following lemma, in which we refer to the properties introduced in Section , clarifies the matters. lemma The properties $\textit{sd}^{\: g}, \ \textit{msd}^{\: g}$ and $\textit{br}^{\: g}$ are monotonic. lemma Straightforward. So Theorem applies to the above three properties. (Note that $\textit{br}^{\: g}$ actually comes in three 'flavours' depending on the choice of beliefs.) Strict dominance in the sense of $\textit{sd}^{\: g}$ is studied in , while $\textit{br}^{\: g}$ corresponds to the rationalizability notion of. To see the consequences of Theorem note the following lemma. lemma The properties $\textit{sd} ^{\: l}, \ \textit{msd} ^{\: l}$ and $\textit{br} ^{\: l}$ satisfy (). lemma Straightforward. So Theorem shows that the `customary' concepts of strict dominance, $\textit{sd} ^{\: l}$ and $\textit{msd} ^{\: l}$ and the 'local' version of the best response property $br ^ l$ cannot be justified in the used epistemic framework as `stand alone' concepts of rationality. Indeed, this theorem shows that common knowledge that each player is rational in one of these three senses does not exclude any strategy. What can be done is to justify these concepts as consequences of the common knowledge of rationality defined in terms of $\textit{br} ^{\: g}$, the `global' version of the best response property, Namely, we have the following result. When each property $\phi_i$ equals $\phi$, we write here $CK({\phi})$ instead of $CK({\overline{\phi}})$ and analogously for $CB$. theorem For all games $H$ \[ G_CK(br^ g) = G_CB(br^ g) T^_sd^ l, \] where we take as the set of beliefs the set of joint strategies of the opponents. theorem By Lemma and Theorem $G_{CK(\textit{br}^{\: g})} = G_{CB(\textit{br}^{\: g})} = T^{\infty}_{\textit{br}^{\: g}}$. Each best response to a joint strategy of the opponents is not strictly dominated, so for all restrictions $G$ \[ T_br^ g(G) T_sd^ g(G) \] and also \[ T_sd^ g(G) T_sd^ l(G). \] So by Lemma $T^_br^ g T^_sd^ l$, which concludes the proof. The above result formalizes and justifies in the epistemic framework used here the often used statement: quote common knowledge of rationality implies that the players will choose only strategies that survive the iterated elimination of strictly dominated strategies quote for games with arbitrary strategy sets and transfinite iterations of the elimination process. In the case of finite games we have the following known result. For a proof using Harsanyi type spaces see. theorem For all finite games $H$ $ G_CK(br^ g) = G_CB(br^ g) T^_msd^ l, $ where we take as the set of beliefs the set of joint mixed strategies of the opponents. theorem The argument is analogous as in the previous proof but relies on a subsidiary result. Again by Lemma and Theorem $G_CK(br^ g) = G_CB(br^ g) = T^_br^ g$. Further, for all restrictions $G$ \[ T_br^ g(G) T_br^ l(G) \] and \[ T_br^ l(G) T_brc^ l(G), \] where ${brc}^{\: l}$ stands for the best response property w.r.t.~the correlated strategies of the opponents. So by Lemma $T^_br^ g T^_brc^ l$. But by the result of [ page 60]OR94 (that is a modification of the original result of ) for all restrictions $G$ we have $T_{\textit{brc}^{\: l}}(G) = T_{\textit{msd}^{\: l}}(G)$, so $T^{\infty}_{\textit{brc}^{\: l}} = T^{\infty}_{\textit{msd}^{\: l}}$, which yields the conclusion.

summary.content: The section discusses the implications of two theorems regarding the properties of strict dominance, mixed strict dominance, and best response in strategic games. It establishes that these properties are monotonic and cannot be justified as standalone concepts of rationality within the given epistemic framework. Instead, they can be derived from the common knowledge of rationality defined by the global best response property. The results formalize the idea that common knowledge of rationality leads players to select strategies that survive the iterated elimination of strictly dominated strategies, particularly in games with arbitrary strategy sets and transfinite iterations. For finite games, a similar conclusion is reached, showing that the best response properties align with mixed strict dominance under the appropriate conditions.

summary.content: The appendix provides a proof of a lemma and a theorem related to strategic games with arbitrary strategy sets. The lemma is established through transfinite induction, demonstrating that for all ordinals $\alpha$, the inclusion \( T_1^{\alpha} \subseteq T_2^{\alpha} \) holds. The theorem is proven by showing three inclusions: (i) \( G_{CK(\overline{\phi})} \subseteq G_{CB(\overline{\phi})} \), (ii) \( G_{CB(\overline{\phi})} \subseteq T_{\overline{\phi}}^{\infty} \), and (iii) \( T_{\overline{\phi}}^{\infty} \subseteq G_{CK(\overline{\phi})} \). The proof utilizes Tarski's Fixpoint Theorem and constructs knowledge correspondences to demonstrate that players are rational in specific states, ultimately establishing the relationships between common knowledge and bounded rationality in the context of the game.

sections.content: Representing and reasoning about qualitative temporal information is an essential part of many artificial intelligence tasks. These tasks appear in such diverse areas as natural language processing, planning, plan recognition, and diagnosis. Allen has proposed an interval algebra framework and Vilain and Kautz have proposed a point algebra framework for representing such qualitative information. All models that have been proposed afterwards in the litterature derive from these two frameworks. Placing two intervals on the Timeline, regardless of their length, gives thirteen relations, known as Allen's relations. Vilain provided relations for points and intervals, Kandrashina provided relations for points, intervals and chains of intervals. Relations between two chains of intervals have been studied in depth by Ladkin who named them non convex intervals. Al-Khatib used a matricial approach. Ligozat has studied relations between chains of points, named generalized intervals. One fundamental reasoning task that arises in applications in these frameworks is given by the following scheme: given possibly indefinite and incomplete knowledge of the relationships between some temporal objects, find the consistent scenarii between all these objects. All these models have in common that the representations of temporal information are depicted as sets of binary relationships and are viewed as binary constraint networks. The reasoning is then based on transitive s that describe the composition of any two binary relations. All these models require transitive s - or similarly inference rules - for solving such tasks. The logical approach of the I.A. community explains this fact. The framework of formal languages, inside which the model of S-languages has been proposed , provides the same material both for expressing the temporal objects and the n-ary relationships between them. The reasoning is based on three natural extensions of very well-known rational operations on languages: the intersection, the shuffle and the projection. More precisely, we have shown in that binary relations between two generalized intervals are in a natural correspondence with S-languages that express Delannoy paths of order 2. By the way, we provide to Henry Delannoy (1833-1915) a large domain of applications (though unexpected) of his theory of minimal paths of the queen from one corner to any other position on a chess-board. The main idea for using formal languages for temporal representation and reasoning is that a word can be viewed as a line, with an arrow from left to right (the way of reading in european languages). Hence, assigning a letter to each temporal object, as its identity, and using as many occurrences of this identity as it has points or interval bounds, it is possible to describe an atomic temporal relation between $n$ objects on the timeline, as far as there is no simultaneity, with a word on an $n$-alphabet (alphabet with $n$ letters). Simultaneity requires to be able to write several letters inside a same box. This is the aim of the theory of S-languages. In this paper, we show how the S-languages framework allows to represent $n$-ary qualitative temporal relations and to reason without any transitive s. In the next part, we recall the basis of formal languages, following , and S-languages, and we examine the usual operations of the relational algebra in the context of S-languages. We then provide two examples of how to reason without transitivity s. The first one is a revisitation of the well-known unsatisfiable closed network of Allen. The second one revisits the Manna-Pnuelli's problem of the allocation of a resource between several requesters. This aims to show how a problem of concurrency for complex systems, written in modal temporal logic can be solved with the S-languages framework.

summary.content: Representing and reasoning about qualitative temporal information is crucial in various AI tasks, including natural language processing and planning. The foundational frameworks for this representation are Allen's interval algebra and Vilain and Kautz's point algebra, which have inspired subsequent models. These models typically rely on binary relationships and transitive relations for reasoning, but this paper introduces a method using S-languages that allows for reasoning without transitive relations. By employing formal languages, the authors demonstrate how to represent n-ary qualitative temporal relations and provide examples, including a revisitation of Allen's unsatisfiable closed network and the Manna-Pnueli resource allocation problem, showcasing the applicability of S-languages in solving concurrency issues in complex systems.

sections.content: Let us first recall some basis on formal languages. Basis An alphabet $X$ is a finite nonempty set of symbols called letters. A word (of length $k \geq 0$) over an alphabet $X$ is a finite sequence $ x_1, \ldots, x_k$ of letters in $ X$. A word $ x_1, \ldots, x_k$ is usually written $ x_1 \ldots x_k$. The unique word having no letter, of length zero, called the empty word, is denoted by $\varepsilon$. The length of a word $f$ is denoted by $ |f|$. The number of occurrences of a letter $a$ in the word $f$ is denoted by $ |f|_a$. The set of all words (resp. of length $n$) on $X$ is denoted by $X^*$ (resp. $ X^n$). Let us remark that $X^* = \bigcup _{ n\geq 0} X^n$. The set of all words on $X$ is written $X^*$. A subset of $X^*$ is called a language. The empty set $\emptyset$ is the least language and $X^*$ is the greatest language for the order of inclusion. Let $u$ and $v$ be words in $X^*$. If $u=u_1 \ldots u_r$ and $v=v_1 \ldots v_s$ are words, then $u.v$ (usually written $uv$), called the concatenation of $u$ and $v$, is the word $u_1 \ldots u_rv_1 \ldots v_s$. For instance let $X=\{ x, y \}$, $u = xx$ and $v = yy$, then the concatenation is $uv = xxyy$. Let us notice that $uv\neq vu$. We also have to set $u^0=\{\varepsilon \}$ , $u^1=u$, $u^{n+1}=uu^n$. One has $v.\varepsilon = \varepsilon .v=v$. The concatenation can be extended to languages on $X$ by setting $L.L'=\{ uv | u\in L, v\in L' \}$. This operation endows $2^{X^*}$ with a structure of non-commutative monoid. We also have $L^0=\{\varepsilon \}$ , $L^1=u$, $L^{n+1}=LL^n$, $L^* = {\bigcup}_ { n\geq 0} L^n$. $u^* = {\bigcup}_ { n\geq 0} u^n$. Even if $u^*$ is a set, it can be worked with like an element, so that we will take this alternative and use $u^*$ as a word or S-word. The shuffle is a very useful operator which is used in concurrency applications. The shuffle operator describes all possibilities of doing two concurrent sequences of actions in a sequential manner. Therefore, this is not a binary combination of $X^*$ because, from two words, it provides a set of words, that is a language. Its definition is the following: Let $u$ and $v$ be two words written on an alphabet $X^*$. The shuffle of $u$ and $v$ is the language $u v= \ \alpha_1\beta_1 \alpha_k\beta_k X^* \alpha_1, \beta_k X^*, \alpha_2, , \alpha_k, \beta_1, , \beta_k-1 X^+, u= \alpha_1 \alpha_k$, $v= \beta_1 \beta_k \ $. For instance let $X=\{ x, y \}$, then $xx yy = \ xxyy, xyxy, yxxy, xyyx, yxyx, yyxx \$. The concatenation $uv$ means an order between $u$ and $v$, this is a word of the language $u \shuf v$. One has $ \varepsilon \shuf v =v \shuf \varepsilon = {v}$ for any word $v$ of $X^*$. The shuffle can be naturally extended to languages on $X$ by setting $L \shuf L' = \bigcup_{u \in L, v\in L'} u\shuf v$. The shuffle endows $2^{X^*}$ with a structure of commutative monoid. Words are read from left to right, so that the reading induces a natural arrow of Time. Any occurrence of a letter can be viewed as an instant numbered by its position inside the word. Traces languages or paths expressions are used for such a purpose: planning the order of execution of events. But with these languages, it is not possible to differentiate two occurrences that are concurrent ( one may be before, at the same time or after the other) from those that must occur at the same time: these two events are said to commute. It is presupposed that the granularity of the time measurement is fine enough to avoid the case at the same time. S-alphabet, S-words, S-languages In order to model explicitly concurrency with words, various tools have been proposed such as event structures or equivalence relations on words traces. In those theories, it is not possible to model only synchronization. One is able to say that two events can be done at the same time but it is not possible to express that they have to be done at the same time. This is due to the fact that concurrency is modelled inside a deeply sequential framework, hence, synchronization is simulated with commutativity. But one has to handle with instant, in the sense of Russell. This is why we introduce the concept of S-alphabet which is a powerset of a usual alphabet. Basic definitions Let us set definition If $X$ is an alphabet, an S-alphabet over $X$ is a non-empty subset of $2^X- \emptyset$. An element of an S-alphabet is an S-letter. A word on an S-alphabet is an S-word. A set of words on an S-alphabet is an S-language. definition S-letters are written either horizontally or vertically: $\ a,b \ =\ a, b, \ a b \ \$. For S-letters with only two letters, we also write $ a b$ instead of $\ a b \ $. Examples of S-alphabets over X are: - the natural one $\dot{X} = \{ \{ a \} |\ a \in X \} $ that is identified with $X$. - the full S-alphabet over $X$, $\widehat{X}= 2^X- \emptyset$. - S-alphabets obtained from others S-alphabets with the following construction: For an S-alphabet $Y$ over $X$, define $Y =\ A | A_1, , A_k Y : A = \bigcup_i=1^k A_i \$. $Y$ is also an S-alphabet over $X$. Note that, for all S-alphabets $Y$ and $Z$ over $X$, we have $\overbrace{\overbrace{Y}}=\overbrace{Y}$ and $\overbrace{\widehat{Y} \cup Z}=\overbrace{Y \cup Z}$. A S-word on a full S-alphabet over $X$ will be simply designed by an S-word on $X$. In this work, we use the full S-alphabet $\widehat{X}= 2^X- \emptyset$. Identifying any singleton with its letter, we write $X \subset \widehat{X}$ and $X^* \subset {\widehat{X}}^{^*}$. In order to link S-words on $X$ with letters of $X$, we set definition Let $X=$x1n be an n-alphabet and $f X^^*$. The S-shuffle has to be generalized in the following way: definition Let $X$ and $Y$ be two disjoint alphabets, $f X^^*$, $g Y^^*$. The S-shuffle of $f$ and $g$ is the language $[f || g]= \ h_1 h_r h_i X Y$, with $max(|f|,|g|) r |f| +|g|$ and such that there are decompositions of $f$ and $g$: $f=f_1\ldots f_k$, $g=g_1 g_k$, satisfying, (i) $\forall i \in [r]$, $ f_i, g_i 1$, (ii) $1\leq |f_i|+|g_i|$, and (iii) $h_i=f_i g_i \.$ definition For instance $[aa || bb]$=$\{ aabb$, $a\left\{ {a \atop b}\right\} b$, $abab,$ $\left\{ {a \atop b}\right\} ab$ ,$ ab \ a b\$, $\ a b\ \ a b\$, $ baab$, $ba \left\{ {a \atop b} \right\} $, $abba$, $\left\{ {a \atop b} \right\} ba$, $baba$, $b \left\{ {a \atop b} \right\} a$, $bbaa \}= \{ f \in \widehat{\{ a,b \} }^* | \vec{f}=(2,2) \}$. The S-shuffle of two S-languages $L$ and $L'$ written on two disjoint alphabets is the language $[L|| L' ]= \cup_f L, f' L' [f || f' ]$. The S-shuffle is, like the shuffle, an associative and commutative operations, which allows to note $[u_1||\cdots ||u_n]$ for the S-shuffle of $n$ S-words or S-languages. In the case where all S-words of a language $\mathcal{L}$ share the same Parikh vector, we note $\vec{\mathcal{L}}$ this common Parikh vector. In particular, on the $n$-alphabet $X=\{x_1, \cdots, x_n\}$, the language, $$\mathcal{L}(p_1, \cdots, p_n)=\{ f \in {\hat{X}}^* | \vec{f}=(p_1, \cdots, p_n)\}$$ that we call $(p_1, \cdots, p_n)$-Delannoy Language -- on $X$ --, are of a particular interest for temporal qualitative reasoning, as we will show it in the next section. Let us just recall that the cardinality $D (p_1, \ldots, p_n)$ of a $(p_1, \cdots, p_n)$-Delannoy Language is given by the following functional equation: $$ D (p_1, \ldots, p_n) = \sum_{\mathcal{P}red(p_1,\ldots,p_n)}  D_n(\widetilde{p_1}, \cdots, \widetilde{p_n})  $$ where for $p>0)$, $\widetilde{p}=\{p, p-1\}$; $\widetilde{0}=\{0\}$ and $Pred((p_1, , p_n)) = \ (p_1, , p_n) \ - \ (p_1, , p_n)\$. A Delannoy path is given as a path that can be drawn on a rectangular grid, starting from the southwest corner, going to the northeast corner, using only three kinds of elementary steps: north, east, and north-east. Hence they are minimal paths with diagonal steps. The natural correspondence between (p,q)-Delannoy paths and $\mathcal{L}(p, q)$ on the alphabet $\{a, b\}$ is: the S-letter $a$ corresponds to a north-step, the S-letter $b$ to a east-step and the S-letter ${ a \choose b}$ to north-east-step. Projection We extend the well-known notion of projection in formal languages theory to S-languages. The aim is to be able to erase all occurrences of some letters in an S-word and having as results a new S-word. The problem is how to handle an S-letter with all its letters erased. summary.content: The section discusses the foundational concepts of formal languages, starting with the definition of an alphabet, words, and languages. It introduces operations such as concatenation and shuffle, which allow for the combination of words and languages, respectively, and highlights the non-commutative nature of concatenation compared to the commutative property of shuffle. The concept of S-alphabets is introduced to explicitly model concurrency, where S-letters and S-words represent elements of these alphabets. Additionally, the section defines the S-shuffle operation and its extension to S-languages, emphasizing its associative and commutative properties. Finally, it presents the notion of Delannoy languages, which are relevant for temporal qualitative reasoning, and outlines the projection operation in the context of S-languages.

sections.section_title: Qualitative Temporal Objects and Relations in the binary algebra and their transitivity tables
sections.content: We examine qualitative temporal objects and relations inside the framework of relational algebra, as Ladkin and Maddux initiated it. We recall the usual qualitative temporal binary algebra: the point algebra, the interval algebra , the point-interval algebra , chains algebra. In this paper, we use the term situation for the description of a unique temporal relation (complete information) between objects, which is sometimes called an atomic relation. Let us recall the principia of transitivity. Given a particular theory $\Sigma$ supporting a set of mutually exhaustive and pairwise disjoint dyadic situations, three individuals, $a$, $b$ and $c$ and a pair of dyadic relations $R_1$ and $R_2$ selected from $\Sigma$ such that $R_1(a,b)$ and $R_2(b,c)$, the transitive closure $R_3(a,c)$ represents a disjunction of all the possible dyadic situations holding between $a$ and $c$ in $\Sigma$. Each $R_3(a,c)$ result can be represented as one entry of a matrix for each $R_1(a,b)$ and $R_2(b,c)$ ordered pair. If there are $n$ dyadic situations supported by $\Sigma$, then there will be $n \times n$ entries in the matrix. This matrix is a transitivity. Transitive s for binary situations have been written for convex intervals (Allen), for points, for points and convex intervals: knowing an atomic relation between objets $A $ and $B$ and an atomic relation between objects $B$ and $C$, derive the possible - or other said not prohibited - relations between objects $A$ and $C$. Cohn have studied transitivity s for reasoning in both time and space in a more general context. They noted the difficulty to build such secure transitivity s. The Point Algebra. The three situations are the three basic temporal relations: before $<$, equals $=$ and after $>$. The set of point qualitative temporal binary relations is the set : $\{ <, >, =, \leqslant , \geqslant , \neq ,\bot ,\top\}$, where $\bot$ is the empty relation (no feasible relation) and $\top$ the universal relation (any relation is feasible). The transitive is given in For instance, if $A<B$ and $B>C$ then~$A\top C$. The Interval Algebra. In , we recall the thirteen situations between two intervals studied by Allen~. The transitivity is given in whereThe notation is taken, whenever possible, from Delannoy paths draw as kind of greek letters on the chess, with the following convention: Upper case for 5-subsets, lower case for 3-subsets: $\Box=\top$, that is there is no constraint, every situation is allowed, $\Diamond=\top - \{ <, m, m^{\sim}, >\}$, which means that the two intervals intersects on an interval, this is exactly what Kamp named the overlappingIn french, couverture relation $\circ$ on two processes and Freksa the contemporary relation , $\Gamma^{\sim}=\{ <, m, o, s, d\}$, that is the relation begin before, $\Lambda=\{ <, m,o, d^{\sim},f^{\sim}\}$, that is the relation end after $\alpha=\{<, m, o\}$, $\delta^{\sim}=\{ o, s, d\}$, $\rho^{\sim}=\{o^{\sim}, d,f\}$, $\hat{s}=\{s, =, s^{\sim}\}$, $\hat{f}=\{f, =, f^{\sim}\}$ and using the following property: $\forall A \subseteq \top, x \in A\ iff \ x^{\sim}\in A^{\sim}$. The Point-Interval Algebra In order to take into account both instantaneous and durative processes, Vilain provided a model with points and intervals. shows the five situations between a point and an interval. Besides the two preceding transitivity s, are needed six more transitivity s: (i) points/intervals-intervals/points, (ii) points/intervals-intervals/intervals, (iii) points/points-points/intervals, (iv) intervals/intervals-intervals/points, (v) inter\-vals/points-points/intervals, (vi) intervals/points-points/points. Chains Algebras The T-model of Kandrashina has three qualitative basic notions: the point, the interval and the sequence of intervals. Situations between two sequences of intervals are derived from situations between intervals. Some frequent situations are shown like the one in : These objects has been revisited and studied for their own by Ladkin under the name of non-convex intervals. Ligozat generalized to sequences of points and/or intervals under the name of generalized intervals. There are 3 situations between two points, 5 between a point and an interval, 13 situations between two intervals, 8989 situations between two sequences of three intervals or two sequences of 6 points. Ladkin [Theorem1]Lad86, proved the number of situations between two chains of intervals is at least exponential in the number of intervals. The exact number of situations between a sequence of $p$ points and a sequence of $q$ points has been provided by [p. 83]BeL89 without doing the connection with Delannoy numbers. Freksa studied transitivity s with respect to convex set of intervals , Randel \& al. have studied transitivity s for reasoning in both time and space in a more general context, both in order to below the complexity rate of the computations. That was also the aim of Vilain who have studied the fragment of the interval algebra, that can be written without disjunction inside the point algebra, based on the fact that relations between intervals can be translated in terms of their bounds, inside the point algebra. An interval $A$ is a couple of its bounds $(a,\bar{a})$ viewed as points they can contain or not, with the constraint $a < \bar{a}$. Situations between intervals are represented in terms of the situations of their bounds: - A is before B iff $a<\bar{a}<b<\bar{b}$ - A meets B iff $a<\bar{a}=b<\bar{b}$ - A overlaps B iff $a<b<\bar{a}<\bar{b}$ - A starts iff B $a=b<\bar{a}<\bar{b}$ - A during iff $b<a<\bar{a}<\bar{b}$ - A finishes iff $b<a<\bar{a}=\bar{b}$ - A equals B iff $a=b < \bar{a}=\bar{b}$.

summary.content: The section discusses qualitative temporal objects and relations within the framework of relational algebra, as established by Ladkin and Maddux. It reviews various qualitative temporal binary algebras, including point algebra, interval algebra, point-interval algebra, and chains algebra, defining "situation" as a unique temporal relation between objects. The concept of transitivity is explored, where the transitive closure of dyadic relations allows for the derivation of possible relations between objects based on known relations. The section also details specific transitivity tables for different types of relations, including those between points and intervals, and highlights the complexity of establishing secure transitivity relations, referencing the work of various researchers in the field.

sections.section_title: Qualitative Temporal Objects and Relations in the S-languages  framework

summary.content: The section discusses the representation of temporal objects and relations within the S-languages framework, where temporal items are characterized as points or maximal convex intervals, each assigned a unique identity. The S-words, formed from these identities, depict the arrangement of temporal items on a timeline, allowing for the description of their relations through specific S-words. Theorems presented establish a correspondence between these relations and Delannoy paths in a lattice structure, highlighting the complexity of operations on these temporal relations, such as integration and composition. The section introduces two new operators—free integration and bounded integration—aimed at simulating relational operations without relying on transitive tables, emphasizing the computational challenges and strategies for improving efficiency in handling these operations.

In temporal applications, information often comes from multiple sources, and when no credibility weights are assigned, the typical approach is to intersect all available information. Vilain and Kautz identified two key problems: determining the resulting set of constraints between two intervals and deducing constraints between two intervals based on transitive relations. The authors present a framework where both problems are addressed similarly, using intersection and integration operators. They derive a main theorem that describes the all-solution problem and the temporal satisfaction problem for a set of temporal items, demonstrating the computation of languages through intersections of various constraints. An example illustrates that the intersection of several languages can lead to an unsatisfiable condition, resulting in an empty language.

Most of the temporal properties of programs have been studied inside either the framework of temporal logics or modal logic. Temporal reasoning about concurrent systems can be partitioned in a natural way into two classes related to the modality used : necessity, symbolized by $\Box$ or possibility, symbolized by $\Diamond$. Translated in a temporal framework, we use the terms always and sometime. These modalities were studied first by the MegariansA school founded by Euclid of Megaric, student of Socrates, like Plato, this school was concurrent of Aristotle's one., then by Aristotle and the Stoic. Despite their variant, these modalities are linked to the universal $ orall$ and particular $\exists$ quantifiers. Manna and Pnuelli , defined three important classes of temporal properties of concurrent programs that are investigated inside the modal temporal framework. They are invariance, liveness and precedence properties. The first two ones are closely related to the two basis modalities $\Box$, which is interpreted as always from now on and $\Diamond$ which is interpreted as $sometimes$ or at least one time from now on. The third one is an extension of the $\Diamond$ class, proposed by Manna and Pnuelli, closed to the $\mathcal{U}$, the until modality in order to capture precedence in general. These three classes are available for temporal properties in general. We first review these three classes and then we revisit their example inside our formal languages framework. Our purpose is not to criticize their solution, but only to translate it inside our model. Temporal properties types The first class is the class of invariance properties. These are properties that can be expressed by a temporal formula of the form: $\Box \psi$ or $\varphi \Rightarrow \Box\psi$. Such a formula, stated for a program $P$, says that every computation of $P$ continuously satisfies $\psi$ throughout the rest of the computation either from the beginning (first formula) or whenever $\varphi$ becomes true. Among properties falling into this class are: partial correctness, error-free behavior, mutual exclusion and absence of deadlocks. The second set, associated to the $sometimes$ modality defines the liveness properties class. These properties are expressible by temporal formulas of the form: $\Diamond \psi$ or $\varphi \Rightarrow \Diamond\psi$. In both cases these formulas guarantee the occurrence of some event $\psi$; in the first case unconditionally and in the second case conditional on an earlier occurrence of the event $\varphi$. Among properties falling into this class are: total correctness, termination, accessibility, lack of individual starvation, and responsiveness. The third class is the precedence properties class which is very well-known inside the artificial intelligence community. In a broad sense, Manna and Pnuelli asserted that precedence properties are all the properties that are expressible using the until operator $\mathcal{U}$ in formulas such as $\chi \mathcal{U} \psi$ or $\varphi \Rightarrow \chi \mathcal{U} \psi$. In both cases the formulas again guarantee the occurrence of the event $\psi$, but they also ensure that from now until that occurrence, $\chi$ will continuously hold. Among properties falling into the until class are strict (FIFO) responsiveness, and bounded overtaking. The meaning they give to the precedence operator, that is to the formula $p<q$, is that $q$ eventually happens, and $p<q$ is automatically satisfied if $q$ never happens. Hence we have: $$p<q \equiv

The Allocation Problem Let us consider a program $G$ (granter) serving as an allocator of a single resource between several processes (requesters) $ R_1, \ldots ,R_k$ competing for the resource. Let each $R_i$ communicate with $G$ by means of two boolean variables: $r_i$ and $g_i$. The variable $r_i$ is set to $ true$ ($=1$) by the requester to signal a request for the resource. Once $R_i$ has the resource it signals its release by setting it to $false$ ($=0$). The allocator G signals $R_i$ that the resource is granted to him by setting $g_i$ to $true$. Having obtained a release signal from $R_i$, which is indicated by $r_i=false$, some time later, it will appropriate the resource by setting $g_i$ to $false$. summary.content: Temporal reasoning about concurrent systems is categorized into two classes based on modality: necessity ($\Box$) and possibility ($\Diamond$), which correspond to "always" and "sometime," respectively. Manna and Pnuelli identified three key classes of temporal properties for concurrent programs: invariance, liveness, and precedence properties. Invariance properties ensure that certain conditions hold throughout the execution of a program, while liveness properties guarantee that specific events will eventually occur. Precedence properties, which can be expressed using the until operator $\mathcal{U}$, ensure that certain conditions hold until an event occurs. The paper also discusses an allocation problem involving a resource allocator and multiple requesters, defining various properties such as responsiveness and FIFO order, and translating these properties into a formal language framework.

sections.content: In this paper, we have presented the S-languages framework and shown how to represent and to reason on qualitative temporal problem. The Hasse Diagram we provide for the allocation problem has to be compared with the temporally labeled graph of Gerevini and Schubert. Different implementations have been made in order to improve the complexity on the computations. They take benefits of the algorithms used for computing operations in formal languages theory, and the use of automata theory. The problems come, as usual, from the parts of S-languages that have to be broken into disjoint parts, in order to go on in the computation. Two implementations has already been made, concerning the interval algebra. The first one is based on the notion of pattern. The second one applies it on the linguistical model of Descl\'es based on topological intervals. Bounds of intervals are labelled in order to mention whether an interval is open or closed. As $ \mathcal{L}(p_1, \cdots, p_n)$ is a lattice, we work on convex parts, following the approach of Freksa. These prototypes suggest that ii may be better to compute in two steps: first accepting all situations, even those not allowed situations, and second without forbidden situations, rather than to compute directly the good solution.

summary.content: This paper introduces the S-languages framework for representing and reasoning about qualitative temporal problems, comparing its Hasse Diagram for the allocation problem with the temporally labeled graph of Gerevini and Schubert. Various implementations have been developed to enhance computational complexity, leveraging algorithms from formal languages theory and automata theory. Challenges arise from the need to partition S-languages into disjoint components for computation. Two implementations focused on interval algebra have been created: one based on patterns and another utilizing Desclés' linguistic model of topological intervals, where interval bounds are labeled as open or closed. The findings suggest a two-step computation approach, first considering all situations and then excluding forbidden ones, rather than directly seeking the optimal solution.
